oneesan.description: Use お姉さん for any young woman addressed politely — a shop clerk, a stranger — not only an actual older sister.

onegaishimasu.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>request</kanji> held out flat in both hands, with <vocabulary>please</vocabulary> set on top like a bow on a box. That polite wrapping around the ask is the whole word.
onegaishimasu.reading_mnemonic: You hold the door for a courier whose arms are stacked with boxes and call <reading>おねがいします</reading>, which lands like <reading>oh, need I ask</reading>. You hardly do, so the word is a light, polite <vocabulary>please</vocabulary>.

ongaku.meaning_mnemonic: Take the kind of <kanji>sound</kanji> that makes you sit up in a silent room and string it along a branch like ice beads until sitting and listening is pure <kanji>comfort</kanji>. That is <vocabulary>music</vocabulary>.

ongakushitsu.meaning_mnemonic: Pack every <kanji>sound</kanji> a school makes into one room where the only <kanji>music</kanji> is on the timetable, and that is the <vocabulary>music room</vocabulary>.

oniisan.meaning_mnemonic: A tired customer at Koichi's konbini calls the teenage clerk an <vocabulary>older brother (polite)</vocabulary> before he even rings up her onigiri, though they have never met.
oniisan.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker clutches his aching <reading>knee</reading> and yells 「<reading>おにいさん</reading>」, begging the <vocabulary>older brother (polite)</vocabulary> leading the group to slow down.
oniisan.description: Use お兄さん for any young man addressed politely — a waiter, a stranger — not only an actual older brother.

onnanohito.meaning_mnemonic: The door meant for any <kanji>person</kanji> gets repainted with a <kanji>woman</kanji> stick figure, so now it specifies exactly which <vocabulary>woman</vocabulary> may enter.
onnanohito.description: 女 alone can sound blunt when pointing at a specific woman; 女の人 is the everyday, polite way to say it in conversation.

onnanoko.meaning_mnemonic: A costume shop sells a miniature <kanji>woman</kanji> outfit sized only for a <kanji>child</kanji>, and whoever fits into it is simply called a <vocabulary>girl</vocabulary>.

ooi.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>many</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>many</vocabulary> word are the same character. The い hooked on the end marks it as an adjective, a habit every い adjective keeps.
ooi.reading_mnemonic: The crowd packed onto the school sports field is so <vocabulary>many</vocabulary> that when they all shout <reading>oi</reading> at once, that <reading>おおい</reading> wall of sound rattles the windows.

ookii.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>big</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>big</vocabulary> word are the same character. The kana tail ending in い is the part that makes it an adjective, and every い adjective after this works the same way.
ookii.reading_mnemonic: A mover tilts a wardrobe off the truck and finds it is too <vocabulary>big</vocabulary> to fit through the front gate. He stands there stuck, muttering <reading>oh, oh, key</reading> — <reading>おおきい</reading>.

oriru.meaning_mnemonic: The chairlift on the mountain trail carries you up, and where the cable turns you <kanji>descend</kanji> from the seat onto the snow. That hop down off the lift is how you <vocabulary>get off</vocabulary>.
oriru.reading_mnemonic: Ori the lift attendant sighs <reading>'oh, really'</reading> at every skier who freezes on the unloading ramp. Only when they hear his flat 「<reading>おりる</reading>」 do they finally <vocabulary>get off</vocabulary> the chair.

orosu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>down</kanji> kanji sits right inside <vocabulary>to lower</vocabulary>, the same downward move. The trailing kana add a pair of hands, so you take hold of a real object and bring it down yourself.
orosu.reading_mnemonic: In Koichi's konbini a crate of frozen <reading>walrus</reading> steaks sits jammed on the top shelf. He wraps both arms around it and works it down to the floor, with a grunt of 「<reading>おろす</reading>」 at every step, until he has <vocabulary>lowered</vocabulary> the whole load.

osake.meaning_mnemonic: Leave cooked rice and clean river water together in a warm, dark cupboard for a few weeks. The mixture quietly ferments into <vocabulary>alcohol / sake</vocabulary>.
osake.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's neighbour <reading>O'Sakey</reading> climbs the mossy steps each evening with one bottle and nothing else. Two cups of <reading>おさけ</reading> later he is asleep among the cats, and the name has stuck to the <vocabulary>alcohol / sake</vocabulary> in his hand.

osewa-ni-naru.meaning_mnemonic: The people of your <kanji form="世">world</kanji> will not stop <kanji form="話">talking</kanji> about whether you have eaten and slept enough. When a whole family keeps you fed and rested like that, you have come <vocabulary form="お世話になる">to be in someone's care</vocabulary>.

oshieru.meaning_mnemonic: You take something you know cold and load it, piece by piece, into a head that did not have it an hour ago. Doing that on purpose, until it sticks in the other person, is what it means to <vocabulary>teach</vocabulary>.
oshieru.reading_mnemonic: A new student in the echoing hallway watches the tutor break every hard idea into clean steps and thinks, <reading>oh, she rules</reading>. The tutor smiles and says 「<reading>おしえる</reading>」, and handing knowledge over like that is what it means to <vocabulary>teach</vocabulary>.

oshiete-morau.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="教">teach</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="教えてもらう">to have (someone) teach</vocabulary> word are the same word, so they carry the same meaning.
oshiete-morau.reading_mnemonic: You already know 教 is 「おし」 from 教える, the verb to teach, so <vocabulary form="教えてもらう">to have (someone) teach</vocabulary> is <reading>おしえてもらう</reading>.

osoi.meaning_mnemonic: You order a hot coffee at Koichi's konbini and it arrives the following Tuesday, cold, with a note apologising. Nobody waits a week for coffee unless the service is <vocabulary>slow / late</vocabulary>.
osoi.reading_mnemonic: A snail on the school field is <reading>oh so</reading> relaxed that the nets come down before it reaches the centre line. By the time it crosses, the field is dark and empty, which is exactly <reading>おそい</reading>, or <vocabulary>slow / late</vocabulary>.

ossharu.meaning_mnemonic: Whatever slow <reading>oh, sure</reading> the old retired professor mutters from his armchair, the whole class copies into their notes as settled fact. Giving a statement that weight because of who spoke it is <vocabulary form="おっしゃる">to say, honorifically</vocabulary>, and the sound is <reading>おっしゃる</reading>.

otearai.meaning_mnemonic: The room set aside for you to <kanji>wash</kanji> your <kanji>hand</kanji> in is the one polite people call the <vocabulary>restroom</vocabulary>.

otokonohito.meaning_mnemonic: Someone asks who that <kanji>person</kanji> is, still out in the field flexing all that power. It's simply the <kanji>man</kanji> you already know, nothing more than a <vocabulary>man</vocabulary>.
otokonohito.description: 男 alone can sound blunt when pointing at a specific man; 男の人 is the everyday, polite way to say it in conversation.

otokonoko.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>man</kanji> in the rice field has a <kanji>child</kanji> copying him, flexing a tiny arm, too small to plow anything. That miniature power alone is what makes a <vocabulary>boy</vocabulary>.

otona.meaning_mnemonic: Once a <kanji>person</kanji> gets <kanji>big</kanji> enough, everyone starts calling them an <vocabulary>adult</vocabulary>.
otona.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, only an <reading>おとな</reading> may ring the great bell, so the cats call the rule keeper <reading>Otto Nana</reading>, guardian of every <vocabulary>adult</vocabulary> visitor.
otona.description: As a な adjective, it takes な directly before the noun it describes, not い like most descriptive words.

otosu.meaning_mnemonic: You fumble your phone above the konbini counter and your fingers open. A hand let it go, so when you <vocabulary>drop</vocabulary> a thing, the fault is yours.
otosu.reading_mnemonic: You met this reading of 落 back in 落ちる, so when a hand is what lets the thing go, <vocabulary>to drop</vocabulary> it is <reading>おとす</reading>.

ototoi.meaning_mnemonic: Count back <kanji>one</kanji> more <kanji>day</kanji> past yesterday and you land on <vocabulary>the day before yesterday</vocabulary>.
ototoi.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank an <reading>otter toy</reading> washes ashore two days late, stamped <reading>おととい</reading> for <vocabulary>the day before yesterday</vocabulary> it went missing.

otousan.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>father</kanji> kanji already means father, and <vocabulary>father (polite)</vocabulary> is simply the respectful way to say that very same word.
otousan.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain trail, your <reading>おとうさん</reading> keeps <reading>towing</reading> your backpack up the last steep stretch. That's just what a <vocabulary>father (polite)</vocabulary> does for you.
otousan.description: Use お父さん to speak to or about someone else's father. For your own father, switch to the plainer 父 when talking to an outsider.

otouto.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, the smallest hiker races ahead of everyone and falls straight into the vending machine at the top. That reckless little kid is exactly a <vocabulary>younger brother</vocabulary>.
otouto.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the team's littlest <vocabulary>younger brother</vocabulary> mascot revs an invisible <reading>auto</reading> down the hallway, yelling 「<reading>おとうと</reading>」 every time he nearly crashes.

otsukaresama.meaning_mnemonic: A workmate drops into a chair looking completely <kanji form="疲">weary</kanji>. You greet that tired person in the polite <kanji form="様">manner</kanji> saved for an honoured guest, and that greeting is <vocabulary form="お疲れ様">thank you for your hard work</vocabulary>.

otsuri.meaning_mnemonic: Pay with a note that is far too big and the cashier lets you <kanji>angle</kanji> a fistful of coins back out of the deal. That catch is your <vocabulary>change (money)</vocabulary>.
otsuri.reading_mnemonic: Koichi at the konbini takes your big note and pushes a heap of coins back across the beeping till. You walk out not <reading>utterly</reading> broke, that heap in your palm being your <vocabulary>change (money)</vocabulary>, 「<reading>おつり</reading>」.

otto.meaning_mnemonic: The one who groans the loudest fixing a leaky faucet at 2 AM is your <vocabulary>husband</vocabulary>.
otto.reading_mnemonic: He trips over the cat and yelps <reading>おっと</reading> every morning. It sounds exactly like <reading>oops</reading>, and that's exactly why he's the <vocabulary>husband</vocabulary>.

owari.meaning_mnemonic: The last stop on the mountain trail, past the vending machine, where the path simply quits, is the <vocabulary>end</vocabulary>.
owari.reading_mnemonic: You already know that sound from 終わる, so the noun for where things stop, <vocabulary>end</vocabulary>, is <reading>おわり</reading>.

owaru.meaning_mnemonic: Follow a road all the way to its <kanji>end</kanji> and there is no more road left to walk. Something that runs itself out like that, with nobody stopping it, is <vocabulary>to finish</vocabulary>.
owaru.reading_mnemonic: A walrus down at the riverbank waits for the very last of the light, then flops onto the final rock with nothing left to do. Say <reading>oh, walrus</reading> and you land on <reading>おわる</reading>, the day come <vocabulary>to finish</vocabulary>.

oya.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>parent</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>parent</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they mean exactly the same thing.
oya.reading_mnemonic: A <vocabulary>parent</vocabulary> at the riverbank spots their child wading out too far and snaps '<reading>oh, ya</reading>, back here now'. That reflex bark of '<reading>おや</reading>' is one only a parent makes.

oyasuminasai.meaning_mnemonic: At lights-out Sei mumbles <reading>おやすみなさい</reading> into the pillow, a slurred <reading>oh-yah-soo-me-nah-sigh</reading> that trails off into a yawn. It is the <vocabulary>good night</vocabulary> you say heading to sleep, not the one you say leaving a room.

oyogeru.meaning_mnemonic: Step off the riverbank into deep water and you do not go under; your limbs already know the strokes. Holding yourself up and moving through the water on your own is what it means that you <vocabulary form="泳げる">can swim</vocabulary>.
oyogeru.reading_mnemonic: You already know 「およ」 from 泳ぐ, so <vocabulary form="泳げる">can swim</vocabulary> simply becomes <reading>およげる</reading>.

oyogu.meaning_mnemonic: A dog dropped into the river flattens out, paddles hard with all four legs, and pushes itself forward across the water. It has started to <vocabulary>swim</vocabulary>.
oyogu.reading_mnemonic: A farmer tips a vat of yogurt down his front at the riverbank and wades in to rinse off. The current grabs him, and now he has to <vocabulary>swim</vocabulary>, spitting out <reading>oh, yogurt</reading>, which comes out as <reading>およぐ</reading>.

pan.meaning_mnemonic: A baker too cheap to buy an oven fries every loaf of <vocabulary>bread</vocabulary> in one battered <reading>pan</reading>. Ask him what it is and he just grunts <reading>パン</reading>.

pasokon.meaning_mnemonic: You tap your <reading>passcode in</reading> and the grey slab wakes up with a low hum. That machine, dead weight until you prove who you are and then able to run your whole day, is the <vocabulary>computer</vocabulary> everyone calls the <reading>パソコン</reading>.

pen.meaning_mnemonic: Stand two hundred <reading>ペン</reading> upright in the mud in a big rectangle and you have fenced off a pig <reading>pen</reading>. Every post in that fence is one <vocabulary>pen</vocabulary>.

piano.meaning_mnemonic: A concert announcer rolls the name of the big lacquered keyboard out slow and grand, <reading>pee-AH-no</reading>, and the lid lifts back off eighty-eight keys. That strung box of felt hammers is a <vocabulary form="ピアノ">piano</vocabulary>, <reading>ピアノ</reading>.

raamen.meaning_mnemonic: The whole stadium stands and chants <reading>rah, men</reading> after the final whistle, then pours out to queue at one steaming stall. What they queue for is a bowl of <vocabulary form="ラーメン">ramen</vocabulary>, <reading>ラーメン</reading>.

raigetsu.meaning_mnemonic: The rice due to <kanji>come</kanji> up won't be ready until one more lap of the <kanji>moon</kanji> finishes, and that lap is <vocabulary>next month</vocabulary>.

rainen.meaning_mnemonic: Another chevron is about to <kanji>come</kanji>, scratched onto the shield-board for a <kanji>year</kanji> that hasn't happened yet: <vocabulary>next year</vocabulary>.

raishuu.meaning_mnemonic: A crop that hasn't <kanji>come</kanji> up yet breaks the surface on the <kanji>week</kanji> after this one, which is exactly <vocabulary>next week</vocabulary>.

rajio.meaning_mnemonic: The crackly play-by-play blaring over every <reading>rodeo</reading> comes out of one dented box wired to a fence post. All voices and no picture, that box is the <vocabulary>radio</vocabulary>, and the hands at the ring just call it the <reading>ラジオ</reading>.

rei.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the annual bell inspection turns up nothing wrong, and the inspector announces the crack count in his most formal voice: <vocabulary>zero (formal)</vocabulary>.
rei.description: 零 marks the formal, technical zero, used in temperatures, exam scores, and official readings, where everyday speech reaches for a plainer word instead.

reizouko.meaning_mnemonic: Keep a cupboard-sized <kanji>storehouse</kanji> <kanji>cool</kanji> around the clock, and that humming little <kanji>warehouse</kanji> in the corner of your kitchen is a <vocabulary>refrigerator</vocabulary>.

rekishi.meaning_mnemonic: Write down every <kanji>passage of time</kanji> a place has lived through, one year stacked on the last, and the finished pile is its <vocabulary>history</vocabulary>.

renraku-suru.meaning_mnemonic: To <vocabulary form="連絡する">contact</vocabulary> someone is to <kanji form="連">join</kanji> your thread to theirs and <kanji form="絡">coil</kanji> the two ends together, so a tug you give is felt at their end.

renshuu-suru.meaning_mnemonic: Running the same scale, the same kick, the same brush stroke over and over until your hands do it without you watching is what it means <vocabulary>to practice</vocabulary>.

resutoran.meaning_mnemonic: Chant it and <reading>「レストラン」</reading> falls apart into <reading>rest, oh, ran</reading>. That is you flopping down to rest because you just ran here starving, and the place that then feeds you is a <vocabulary>restaurant</vocabulary>.

rieki.meaning_mnemonic: After every bill is paid and the wages are out the door, the money still sitting in the drawer that the owner keeps for good is <vocabulary form="利益">profit</vocabulary>.

rippa.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji form="派">faction</kanji> that can <kanji form="立">stand</kanji> tall on its own, propped up by nothing, is an impressive thing, and impressive is exactly <vocabulary form="立派">splendid / fine</vocabulary>. It is a な adjective, so な slots in ahead of the noun it describes.

risaikuru.meaning_mnemonic: <reading>Lisa cycles</reading> one loop over and over: bottle bank, crusher, shop, back to the bottle bank. Running that same can around the circle until it becomes a brand-new can is <vocabulary form="リサイクル">recycling</vocabulary>, the loop you hear in <reading>リサイクル</reading>.

riyuu.meaning_mnemonic: A toddler shoves a plant pot off the sill, meets your eyes, and plainly had a <vocabulary>reason</vocabulary>. You are never going to find out what it was.

roku-v.meaning_mnemonic: Nothing was ever added to the <kanji>six</kanji> kanji, so the <vocabulary>six</vocabulary> word is just that same kanji standing alone.

ryokan.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>building</kanji> that fills only with people partway through a <kanji>trip</kanji>, then empties again the morning they move on, is an <vocabulary>inn</vocabulary>.

ryokou.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>trip</kanji> stays a daydream until the two of you follow the banner to the crossroads and actually <kanji>go</kanji>. Once your feet move, that is <vocabulary>trip / travel</vocabulary>.

ryokou-suru.meaning_mnemonic: Shoulder your pack for a <kanji>trip</kanji> and keep choosing to <kanji>go</kanji> at every crossroads, one town after the next. Staying on the move like that, wherever the road forks, is what it is <vocabulary>to travel</vocabulary>.

ryouri.meaning_mnemonic: Raw <kanji>materials</kanji> on the counter mean nothing until you add <kanji>logic</kanji> about heat, water and timing. That worked-out plan for the ingredients is <vocabulary>cooking</vocabulary>.

ryouri-suru.meaning_mnemonic: You take raw <kanji>materials</kanji> and run them through the strict <kanji>logic</kanji> of a recipe, step after step. When that turns them into a hot meal, you <vocabulary>cook</vocabulary>.

ryoushuu.meaning_mnemonic: Once the shop has <kanji form="収">reaped</kanji> your payment into its own <kanji form="領">territory</kanji>, it hands you a slip proving the money changed hands. That slip is a <vocabulary form="領収">receipt</vocabulary>.

ryoushuusho.meaning_mnemonic: Your money crosses into the shop's <kanji>dominion</kanji>, and they <kanji>take it in</kanji> as payment now settled. The slip they <kanji>write</kanji> to prove that changed hands is your <vocabulary>receipt</vocabulary>.

sabishii.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji here already means <kanji>loneliness</kanji> all by itself, and the い on the end makes it the adjective <vocabulary>lonely</vocabulary>.
sabishii.reading_mnemonic: A hiker reaches the mountain trail's one vending machine and finds it sold out, with nobody there to grumble to. The thin '<reading>sob, she</reading>' sound she makes then, '<reading>さびしい</reading>', is exactly how <vocabulary>lonely</vocabulary> feels.

sagaru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>down</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to go down</vocabulary> verb are one and the same direction. With the trailing kana it becomes the verb for that drop happening by itself, with no hand on it.
sagaru.reading_mnemonic: High on the mountain trail a rain-soaked <reading>saguaro</reading> cactus can no longer hold up its arms. One heavy limb sags lower and lower on its own, with a dry rasp of 「<reading>さがる</reading>」, and that slow droop is what it means to <vocabulary>fall</vocabulary>.

sagasu.meaning_mnemonic: Your ring slips off at the riverbank and vanishes into the reeds, so now you are on your knees parting every stalk. Going over a place inch by inch after one lost thing is what it means <vocabulary>to search for</vocabulary> it.
sagasu.reading_mnemonic: A reader wants the old Norse <reading>sagas</reading>, and the librarian is up the ladder again, running one finger along the spines. Combing a whole wall of shelves for a single book is 「<reading>さがす</reading>」, <vocabulary>to search for</vocabulary> it.

sai-age.meaning_mnemonic: Every birthday you get through stacks one more ring of <kanji>age</kanji> onto the pile inside you. Count the rings in that stack and the number is how many <vocabulary>years old</vocabulary> you are.

saichuu.meaning_mnemonic: When an action reaches its <kanji form="最">most</kanji> intense point, you are as deep <kanji form="中">inside</kanji> it as you can get, right <vocabulary form="最中">in the middle of</vocabulary> it.

saifu.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Wealth</kanji> in your pocket is just loose paper and coins. Fold a scrap of <kanji>cloth</kanji> around it and the closed pouch is a <vocabulary>wallet</vocabulary>.

saigo.meaning_mnemonic: Let your <kanji>behind</kanji> foot drag as far back as a foot can possibly go, out to the <kanji>utmost</kanji> extreme. That trailing spot is the <vocabulary>last / end</vocabulary> of the line.

saigo-ni.meaning_mnemonic: Take <kanji form="後">behind</kanji> and push it to the <kanji form="最">utmost</kanji>, the place the trailing foot never catches up from. Acting from that spot, after everyone else has gone, is <vocabulary form="最後に">finally / lastly</vocabulary>.

saikin.meaning_mnemonic: Out of all past time, the stretch sitting <kanji form="近">near</kanji>est to right now is the <kanji form="最">most</kanji> current one. Whatever happened inside it happened <vocabulary form="最近">recently</vocabulary>.

saisho.meaning_mnemonic: Shove your way to the <kanji>utmost</kanji> front of the queue, as far forward as a person can stand. That spot at the very head of everything is the <vocabulary>first / beginning</vocabulary>.

saito.meaning_mnemonic: You tap in an address and a whole shop unfolds where your blank screen was, shelves and counter and a visitor book by the door. A <reading>sight</reading> you can step into like that is a <vocabulary form="サイト">website</vocabulary>, and it goes by <reading>サイト</reading>.

saizu.meaning_mnemonic: The tailor runs the tape around your chest, reads the number, and <reading>sighs</reading>. That number, how big your clothes have to be, is your <reading>サイズ</reading>, your <vocabulary form="サイズ">size</vocabulary>.

sakana.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>fish</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>fish</vocabulary> word are the same, so they mean the same thing.
sakana.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, Ana wrings out a soaking wet <reading>sock</reading> and a live <vocabulary>fish</vocabulary> drops out of the heel. Ana's sock full of fish is <reading>さかな</reading>.

sakkaa.meaning_mnemonic: A striker drops one shoulder and the goalkeeper lunges the wrong way like a <reading>sucker</reading>. Ninety minutes of fooling the last defender like that is <vocabulary form="サッカー">soccer</vocabulary>, <reading>サッカー</reading>.

samui.meaning_mnemonic: The final い makes this an adjective, so you can pin it straight onto a noun. Picture a flat grey sky with your breath hanging in the air and the puddles frozen hard, and that whole outdoor chill is <vocabulary>cold (weather)</vocabulary>.
samui.reading_mnemonic: A courier named <reading>Sam</reading> restocks the mountain-trail vending machine at dawn, hopping and hugging himself. He groans about why it is always this <reading>さむい</reading>, and the frost-white empty trail around him is <vocabulary>cold (weather)</vocabulary> in one picture.

san-v.meaning_mnemonic: There's no gap between the <kanji>three</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>three</vocabulary> word — write one and you've written the other.

sandoicchi.meaning_mnemonic: The picnic filling is so gritty it is like <reading>sand, which</reading> has worked its way between two thick slabs of bread. That gritty stack is a <vocabulary form="サンドイッチ">sandwich</vocabulary>, <reading>サンドイッチ</reading>.

sanka.meaning_mnemonic: You stop watching from the side and start <kanji form="参">going</kanji> along with the group. Once you <kanji form="加">add</kanji> yourself to the people actually doing the thing, that is <vocabulary form="参加">participation (noun)</vocabulary>.

sanka-suru.meaning_mnemonic: Just <kanji form="参">coming</kanji> along to the event is only half of it; once your name is <kanji form="加">add</kanji>ed to the sign-in sheet, you <vocabulary form="参加する">participate</vocabulary>.

sanpo-suru.meaning_mnemonic: Your feet stop flat every few steps and the path just <kanji>scatters</kanji> wherever it likes, aiming nowhere. A <kanji>walk</kanji> that loose and unplanned is you choosing to <vocabulary>take a walk</vocabulary>.

sara.meaning_mnemonic: A shallow ceramic circle you heap food onto and later scrape clean is a <vocabulary>plate / dish</vocabulary>.
sara.reading_mnemonic: At the buffet every <reading>salad</reading> is carried out on its own wide white 「<reading>さら</reading>」, the only <vocabulary>plate / dish</vocabulary> broad enough to hold it.

sara-ni.meaning_mnemonic: On your first morning the manager lists the small perks, then adds one more item on top, the <reading>salary</reading>. Stacking that extra point onto what was already said is <reading>さらに</reading>, <vocabulary form="さらに">furthermore</vocabulary>.

sarada.meaning_mnemonic: The gardener <reading>Sarah Da</reading> tips raw leaves, sliced tomato and cold cucumber into one big wooden bowl and tosses them with oil. That cold raw bowl is a <vocabulary form="サラダ">salad</vocabulary>, <reading>サラダ</reading>.

saru.meaning_mnemonic: A grey shape drops onto the trailhead vending machine, pops the flap with quick clever fingers and swings back up a pine with a stolen can. Only a <vocabulary form="猿">monkey</vocabulary> robs a machine like that.
saru.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank a <vocabulary form="猿">monkey</vocabulary> snatches <reading>a sarong</reading> off the drying line and wears it up a tree. The washer-woman shakes her fist and yells 「<reading>さる</reading>」.

sashiageru.meaning_mnemonic: Noticing the <kanji form="差">difference</kanji> in rank between you and the higher-ranked person, you raise the gift <kanji form="上">up</kanji> with both arms so it travels toward them. Handing something upward across that gap is to <vocabulary form="差し上げる">give, humbly</vocabulary>.

sassoku.meaning_mnemonic: Set <kanji form="早">early</kanji> next to <kanji form="速">quick</kanji> and you get fast piled on fast, the sun barely over the hills and you are already moving. Doing a thing that far ahead of the clock is doing it <vocabulary form="早速">immediately / promptly</vocabulary>.

sassoku-desu-ga.meaning_mnemonic: The sun is barely <kanji form="早">early</kanji>-morning high and you are already moving <kanji form="速">quick</kanji> on the job. Starting with no small talk like that is <vocabulary form="早速ですが">getting right to it</vocabulary>.

satou.meaning_mnemonic: Tip the bag and it hisses out like dry <kanji>sand</kanji>. A spoonful of that pale grit turns your coffee sweet, so it has to be <vocabulary>sugar</vocabulary>.

satsu-counter.meaning_mnemonic: You count anything bound between covers, from novels to textbooks to thin manga, by sliding them onto a shelf one spine at a time. The number of spines lined up in a row is how many <vocabulary>books</vocabulary> you have.

sayounara.meaning_mnemonic: Draw it out on the platform as the train pulls away, the way you would a slow <reading>so long</reading>. That heavy, drawn-out <reading>さようなら</reading> is the <vocabulary>goodbye</vocabulary> that means a good while.
sayounara.description: Heavier than the English 'bye'. It suggests a long separation, so to family or coworkers you will see tomorrow it can sound oddly final; day-to-day partings use lighter phrases.

seetaa.meaning_mnemonic: Pull the thick wool top down over your head and within a minute you start to <reading>sweat</reading>. The heavy knitted layer that does that to you is a <reading>セーター</reading>, a <vocabulary form="セーター">sweater</vocabulary>.

seifu.meaning_mnemonic: Pile every <kanji>government office</kanji> in the country into one enormous building, and whoever ends up running that building is the <vocabulary>government</vocabulary>.

seifuku.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="制">rule</kanji> book fixes every piece of this <kanji form="服">clothing</kanji>, down to the buttons. The one outfit you never get to choose for yourself is a <vocabulary form="制服">uniform</vocabulary>.

seiji.meaning_mnemonic: <vocabulary>Politics</vocabulary> is the whole endless job of trying to <kanji>govern</kanji> a country full of shouting people and somehow get them to <kanji>calm down</kanji>.

seikaku.meaning_mnemonic: Your inborn <kanji form="性">nature</kanji> gets worn over years into a fixed <kanji form="格">rank</kanji> of habits and set reactions. That settled shape is what others call your <vocabulary form="性格">personality</vocabulary>.

seikatsu.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji form="生">life</kanji> seen as the <kanji form="活">lively</kanji>, day-to-day business of eating, washing and getting by is your <vocabulary form="生活">life / living</vocabulary>.

seikou-suru.meaning_mnemonic: Effort that finally <kanji form="成">turns into</kanji> a solid <kanji form="功">achievement</kanji>, a result you can point at, is what it means to <vocabulary form="成功する">succeed</vocabulary>.

seinen.meaning_mnemonic: A man in a <kanji>blue</kanji> shirt who has lived only twenty <kanji>year</kanji>s is a <vocabulary>youth (young man)</vocabulary>.

seinenki.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>person</kanji> the law finally counts as having <kanji>turned into</kanji> a full-grown one is an <vocabulary>adult</vocabulary>.

seito.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>life</kanji> still in its <kanji>junior</kanji> stage, trailing a few steps behind the teacher, is a <vocabulary>pupil</vocabulary>.

sekai.meaning_mnemonic: The people of one <kanji>generation</kanji>, sealed together inside a single <kanji>boundary</kanji> of years, all live in one <vocabulary>world</vocabulary>.

seki.meaning_mnemonic: A hard bark of air fires up your throat with no warning and rattles the whole quiet room. That sharp, helpless burst is a <vocabulary form="咳">cough</vocabulary>.
seki.reading_mnemonic: Koichi tears open a <reading>sack</reading> of flour at the konbini and breathes the white cloud straight in. It punches out a <reading>せき</reading> loud enough to stop the beeping till, because a chestful of flour always ends in a <vocabulary form="咳">cough</vocabulary>.

seki-seat.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine has one dry step among twenty wet ones. Whoever loses the dawn scramble for it loses their <vocabulary>seat</vocabulary>.

sekken.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>stone</kanji>-hard bar that gives up its <kanji>saltiness</kanji> as slippery lather the moment it meets water is <vocabulary>soap</vocabulary>.

semai.meaning_mnemonic: You meet someone in the shrine hallway and you both have to turn sideways to squeeze past, because the walls sit that close together. A passage like that is <vocabulary>narrow / cramped</vocabulary>, and the final い makes it an adjective.
semai.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>semi</reading> truck noses into the alley behind Koichi's konbini and stops dead, wedged tight between the two walls. The alley is <reading>せまい</reading>, far too <vocabulary>narrow / cramped</vocabulary> for a truck that size.

sen-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>thousand</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>thousand</vocabulary> word are one and the same character, doing double duty as itself.

sengetsu.meaning_mnemonic: The one already <kanji>ahead</kanji> of you finished its <kanji>moon</kanji>-lap before you did, and that finished lap is <vocabulary>last month</vocabulary>.

senmonka.meaning_mnemonic: Build your whole <kanji>house</kanji> up against one <kanji>gate</kanji> and refuse to deal with anything outside that single <kanji>specialty</kanji>, and you are a <vocabulary>specialist</vocabulary>.

sensei.meaning_mnemonic: Someone whose <kanji>life</kanji> is already <kanji>ahead</kanji> of yours on the path knows the way, which makes them your <vocabulary>teacher</vocabulary>.

senshuu.meaning_mnemonic: Whoever strode <kanji>ahead</kanji> already crossed the <kanji>week</kanji> before this one, and that finished lap is <vocabulary>last week</vocabulary>.

sentaku-suru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>wash</kanji> here is not the dishes and not your hands, but a heaped basket of dirty shirts and socks. That one narrowed-down job is exactly what it means to <vocabulary>do laundry</vocabulary>.

setsumei.meaning_mnemonic: Take a rough <kanji form="説">theory</kanji> and make every step of it <kanji form="明">bright</kanji> enough for anyone to follow, and what you have handed them is an <vocabulary form="説明">explanation</vocabulary>.

setsumei-suru.meaning_mnemonic: You hold your <kanji>theory</kanji> up and keep rephrasing it until it goes <kanji>bright</kanji> in the other person's head. Making it light up like that is how you <vocabulary>explain</vocabulary> it.

shachou.meaning_mnemonic: Follow the chain of command in a <kanji form="社">company</kanji> all the way up to the one <kanji form="長">leader</kanji> with nobody above them, and that person is the <vocabulary form="社長">company president</vocabulary>.

shain.meaning_mnemonic: Put one more <kanji form="員">member</kanji> on a <kanji form="社">company</kanji>'s payroll, paid from its own account, and that person is now a <vocabulary form="社員">company employee</vocabulary>.

shakai.meaning_mnemonic: Every <kanji>company</kanji> and shrine keeps its gates open, and the crowds who <kanji>meet</kanji> and mingle between them are what we call a <vocabulary>society</vocabulary>.

shakkin.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="金">money</kanji> you <kanji form="借">borrow</kanji> today and keep putting off paying back, month after month, is your <vocabulary form="借金">debt</vocabulary>.

shashin.meaning_mnemonic: Freeze one moment as a <kanji>true</kanji> copy, exact enough that nobody can deny it happened. That undeniable copy of real life is a <vocabulary>photograph</vocabulary>.

shatsu.meaning_mnemonic: You button the cloth from collar to hem until it <reading>shuts</reading> flat against your chest. That sealed panel of fabric you tuck into your trousers is a <vocabulary>shirt</vocabulary>, the one you call 「<reading>シャツ</reading>」.

shi-city.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>city</kanji> kanji standing on its own is the whole word, so this <vocabulary>city</vocabulary> means exactly what the kanji does.

shi-num.meaning_mnemonic: Four (alt) is simply the <kanji>four</kanji> kanji on its own, so the kanji and the <vocabulary>four (alt)</vocabulary> word mean exactly the same thing.

shiawase.meaning_mnemonic: A stalk you raised yourself, coming up green through your own patch of earth, is the small sure <kanji form="幸">happiness</kanji> of being <vocabulary form="幸せ">happy / fortunate</vocabulary>. It works as a な adjective, so な sits before the noun.
shiawase.reading_mnemonic: The woman on the bench gives a small wave at nothing whenever her luck turns. That reflex, <reading>she waves</reading>, is <reading>しあわせ</reading>, the tell of someone <vocabulary form="幸せ">happy / fortunate</vocabulary>.

shibaraku.meaning_mnemonic: A <reading>Shiba</reading> flops onto the warm shrine step, decides to <reading>relax</reading>, and does not budge again for a good long stretch. That nap is how long <reading>しばらく</reading> lasts, and it means <vocabulary form="しばらく">for a while</vocabulary>.

shichi-num.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>seven</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>seven (alt)</vocabulary> word are one and the same, meaning exactly what the kanji already taught you.

shidai-ni.meaning_mnemonic: Work through the list in <kanji form="次">order</kanji>, moving from one <kanji form="第">number</kanji> to the next, and the whole thing shifts <vocabulary form="次第に">gradually</vocabulary>.

shigen.meaning_mnemonic: The underground <kanji>source</kanji> a country pulls its ore, timber, oil and fresh water from is the whole of its <vocabulary>resources</vocabulary>.

shigoto.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>matter</kanji> you loyally <kanji>attend</kanji> to day after day, sandals fetched and tea poured, is your <vocabulary>work / job</vocabulary>.

shigotoba.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>place</kanji> you show up to each day to <kanji>attend</kanji> to the <kanji>business</kanji> that pays you, fetching and carrying until closing, is your <vocabulary>workplace</vocabulary>.

shiharau.meaning_mnemonic: Handing a shop the exact money you owe helps <kanji form="支">support</kanji> it for another day. The formal verb for passing that money across the counter is <vocabulary form="支払う">to pay</vocabulary>.

shijou.meaning_mnemonic: Hand the awning-covered <kanji>market</kanji> one permanent <kanji>place</kanji> to set up, the same square every single day, and that fixed trading ground is a <vocabulary>market</vocabulary>.
shijou.description: Read this way, the word means an abstract market — a stock market, an export market, the whole arena of buyers and sellers. It is not a physical hall of stalls; that sense is a different reading of the same two characters.

shikarareru.meaning_mnemonic: Knock a jar off Grandma Kane's shelf and every cat goes still while she turns and scolds you in a long, rising voice. Standing there and taking all of it is what it means <vocabulary form="叱られる">to be scolded</vocabulary>.
shikarareru.reading_mnemonic: You already know 「しか」 from 叱る, so the version done to you, <vocabulary form="叱られる">to be scolded</vocabulary>, is <reading>しかられる</reading>.

shikaru.meaning_mnemonic: A kid tips a full tray of paint across the floor, and the teacher kneels down and tells him in a hard, flat voice that this was not okay. Speaking to someone that sharply about what they did wrong is what it means <vocabulary form="叱る">to scold</vocabulary>.
shikaru.reading_mnemonic: Each wrong answer earns one more tap of <reading>chalk</reading> on the desk while the teacher lists your mistakes in a rising voice. That steady, sharp correction for a fault is 「<reading>しかる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="叱る">to scold</vocabulary>.

shikashi.meaning_mnemonic: The <reading>cashier</reading> rings up your jackpot ticket with a straight face, <reading>しかし</reading> the drawer slides open on nothing but paperclips. That hard turn from win to nothing is what <vocabulary>however</vocabulary> does to a sentence.

shiken.meaning_mnemonic: A single formal <kanji>try</kanji> that the school scores, records, and later holds against your name is an <vocabulary>exam</vocabulary>.

shiken-o-ukeru.meaning_mnemonic: To <vocabulary form="試験を受ける">take an exam</vocabulary> is to sit still and <kanji form="受">undergo</kanji> a <kanji form="試">test</kanji> that <kanji form="験">examines</kanji> every corner of what you know, one hard question after the next.

shima.meaning_mnemonic: A scrap of land with open sea on every side of it, no bridge and no road off, is an <vocabulary form="島">island</vocabulary>.
shima.reading_mnemonic: Shig the shipwrecked sailor rows for days toward a green <reading>shimmer</reading> on the horizon. When he drags his boat ashore he names the place 「<reading>しま</reading>」, his own <vocabulary form="島">island</vocabulary>.

shimeru.meaning_mnemonic: When the last class leaves, the caretaker at Sei's school walks the hallway pulling every window down and easing every classroom door shut. Bringing something that stood open back to shut is <vocabulary>to close</vocabulary> it.
shimeru.reading_mnemonic: A hard white <reading>shimmer</reading> bounces off the gym windows and blinds every free throw at Sei's school. So the coach sends a player <vocabulary>to close</vocabulary> <reading>しめる</reading> the blinds before practice.

shinbun.meaning_mnemonic: A <vocabulary>newspaper</vocabulary> gathers everything <kanji>new</kanji> that people around town managed to <kanji>hear</kanji>. By morning the whole pile is printed on your doorstep.

shinbun-sha.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>company</kanji> whose one job is to <kanji>hear</kanji> what happened overnight and rush it into print while the news is still <kanji>new</kanji> is a <vocabulary>newspaper company</vocabulary>.

shinchou.meaning_mnemonic: Stand a <kanji form="身">person</kanji> against the wall and measure how <kanji form="長">long</kanji> they are from heel to crown. That measurement is their <vocabulary form="身長">height (body)</vocabulary>.

shinjiru.meaning_mnemonic: To take another person's word as plain <kanji form="信">truth</kanji>, with no proof in your hand, is to <vocabulary form="信じる">believe</vocabulary> them.

shinpai-suru.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>heart</kanji> gets <kanji>parcelled out</kanji>, a scrap of it pinned to every bad thing that might happen. Carry it stretched that thin and you <vocabulary>worry</vocabulary>.

shinsetsu.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>parent</kanji> who <kanji>cuts</kanji> the carrots on your plate into small, easy pieces is being <vocabulary>kind</vocabulary>. Treat it as a な adjective and slip な in before the noun it describes.

shinu.meaning_mnemonic: Everything that was keeping you going, heartbeat, breath, the warmth in your hands, switches off one part at a time and does not come back. That final shutdown is what it means to <vocabulary>die</vocabulary>.

shio.meaning_mnemonic: One shake of the white grit makes hot chips worth eating. The same pinch stings like fire in a small cut, because it is <vocabulary>salt</vocabulary>.
shio.reading_mnemonic: Sho the gull cracks white crystals off the <reading>seashore</reading> rocks with her beak. Each crunch sounds like <reading>しお</reading>, and every flake is pure <vocabulary>salt</vocabulary>.

shippai-suru.meaning_mnemonic: When a plan ends and all it has produced is <kanji form="失">error</kanji>, with no gain left standing, that is what it means to <vocabulary form="失敗する">fail</vocabulary>.

shiraseru.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>know</kanji> a fact the moment your arrow thuds into the target. Firing that same fact into someone else's target is <vocabulary>to inform / notify</vocabulary> them.
shiraseru.reading_mnemonic: You already learned 知 is 「し」 back in 知る, so <vocabulary>to inform / notify</vocabulary> someone is just <reading>しらせる</reading>.

shiro-color.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>white</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>white</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so the meaning carries straight across with nothing added.
shiro-color.reading_mnemonic: Down on the riverbank a rower grips the oars so hard that her knuckles go bloodless <vocabulary>white</vocabulary>. Watch <reading>she rows</reading>, and on every stroke she grunts <reading>しろ</reading>.

shiroi.meaning_mnemonic: This is just the <kanji>white</kanji> kanji you already know, so the <vocabulary>white</vocabulary> word means exactly that and no more. The い on the end is the adjective ending, letting the word describe a noun directly.
shiroi.reading_mnemonic: You already know 白 is read 「しろ」 from the word 白, so once you add an い it becomes <reading>しろい</reading>, the describing word for <vocabulary>white</vocabulary>.

shiru.meaning_mnemonic: Once a fact is stuck to you firmly enough that you can produce it the second someone asks, it is yours. Carrying it around like that, always within reach, is what it means to <vocabulary>know</vocabulary> it.
shiru.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail a <reading>shrew</reading> always taps the one vending-machine button that still works. It squeaks 「<reading>しる</reading>」 at the gaping hiker, and having a fact locked down and ready like that is what it means to <vocabulary>know</vocabulary> it.

shita-v.meaning_mnemonic: This is just the <kanji>down</kanji> kanji you have met, used on its own as the word <vocabulary>down</vocabulary>.
shita-v.reading_mnemonic: The fastest thing at Sei's school is the cheetah hiding <vocabulary>down</vocabulary> under the bleachers, belly flat to the concrete. Nobody checks that low, so it never gets tagged: <reading>cheetah</reading>, <reading>した</reading>.

shitsumon.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school the gate won't open until you answer the <kanji>question</kanji> shouted through its bars. Take that same demand for an answer indoors, hand raised, and you are asking a <vocabulary>question</vocabulary>.

shitsumon-suru.meaning_mnemonic: Walk up to the shouting gate at the school and throw its own <kanji>question</kanji> straight back through the bars at it. Flinging a question at something to force it to talk is what it is <vocabulary>to ask a question</vocabulary>.

shitsurei-shimasu.meaning_mnemonic: Stepping into someone's office is a tiny <kanji form="失">fault</kanji> against the full <kanji form="礼">bow</kanji> of good manners. shitsurei-suru.meaning_mnemonic: You let a small <kanji>fault</kanji> creep into the <kanji>bow</kanji> you owe the room, then slip toward the door. Naming that little rudeness out loud before you go is how you <vocabulary>excuse yourself</vocabulary>.

shiyakusho.meaning_mnemonic: The one <kanji form="所">place</kanji> in the <kanji form="市">city</kanji> where every civic <kanji form="役">duty</kanji> gets handled — a birth registered, a tax paid, a form filed — is the <vocabulary form="市役所">city hall</vocabulary>.

shizen.meaning_mnemonic: Anything that is the way it is by its own <kanji form="自">self</kanji>, just that <kanji form="然">sort of thing</kanji> with nobody shaping it, is <vocabulary form="自然">nature</vocabulary>.

shizuka.meaning_mnemonic: Deep in the school library at exam time, forty students hold so still you can hear the wall clock two rooms away. That held breath, not one creaking chair in it, is <vocabulary>quiet</vocabulary>.
shizuka.reading_mnemonic: The students call the library's silence-warden <reading>She's-a-cop</reading> because she books you for breathing too loud. One look from her and the whole room drops <vocabulary>quiet</vocabulary>, and that hush is <reading>しずか</reading>.

shizumu.meaning_mnemonic: A slow leak fills the rowboat until it tips its nose down and slides under the lake, and the water closes flat over the top. A heavy thing dropping below the surface and staying there is what it is to <vocabulary form="沈む">sink</vocabulary>.
shizumu.reading_mnemonic: The free diver breathes out, whispers 「<reading>she zooms</reading>」, and drops straight down to the dark lake bed. Going under the water and staying down there is what it means to <vocabulary form="沈む">sink</vocabulary>, 「<reading>しずむ</reading>」.

shokuji.meaning_mnemonic: On its own, <kanji>food</kanji> is just stuff on a shelf. Make a whole <kanji>matter</kanji> of it, with plates, chopsticks and a set table, and it becomes a <vocabulary>meal</vocabulary>.

shokuji-suru.meaning_mnemonic: When <kanji>eating</kanji> stops being a quick bite standing up and turns into a sat-down, several-course <kanji>affair</kanji>, you <vocabulary>dine</vocabulary>.

shomei.meaning_mnemonic: A page cannot see your face, so you prove it is you by writing your <kanji form="名">name</kanji> across the bottom in your own hand. That mark is your <vocabulary form="署名">signature</vocabulary>.

shoppai.meaning_mnemonic: Bite into a <reading>shop pie</reading> from the konbini and the filling is pure seawater. That sting is <reading>しょっぱい</reading>, painfully <vocabulary form="しょっぱい">salty</vocabulary>, and the い ending marks it as a describing word.
