tamago.meaning_mnemonic: The smooth white thing in the carton that cracks if you look at it wrong and turns into breakfast the moment it hits a hot pan is an <vocabulary>egg</vocabulary>.
tamago.reading_mnemonic: A hen at Grandma Kane's shrine has started laying one <reading>tomato</reading>-red <vocabulary>egg</vocabulary> every morning on the mossy step. A hen dropping tomatoes is your hook for <reading>たまご</reading>.

tanomu.meaning_mnemonic: You catch your neighbour at the gate, hold out your spare key, and ask her to feed the cat while you are gone. Putting a task in someone else's hands and counting on them to do it is what it means <vocabulary form="頼む">to request / rely on</vocabulary>.
tanomu.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail you feed the lone vending machine your last coins and say <reading>ta</reading> before it even answers. It only hums, so you ask again, staking the whole climb on that one machine working, and that is 「<reading>たのむ</reading>」, <vocabulary form="頼む">to request / rely on</vocabulary>.

tanoshii.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>music</kanji> those ice beads shake out of the bare branches turns a cold walk into something <vocabulary>fun / enjoyable</vocabulary>. That final い is what makes it an adjective.
tanoshii.reading_mnemonic: Tara comes home from the riverbank with a deep <reading>tan — oh, she</reading> had a <vocabulary>fun / enjoyable</vocabulary> day out there. Say <reading>たのしい</reading> and you can hear her showing the tan off.

taoru.meaning_mnemonic: Stack every dry one from the riverbank into a swaying <reading>tower</reading>, and each 「<reading>タオル</reading>」 you peel off the top is one <vocabulary>towel</vocabulary>.

tasukaru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="助">help</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="助かる">to be saved / helped</vocabulary> word are the same. This ending flips it around so the help lands on you, and you are the one pulled clear, not the one doing the pulling.
tasukaru.reading_mnemonic: You go through the ice at the riverbank and a walrus hooks both <reading>tusks</reading> under your arms and heaves you onto the bank. Being lifted clear by something outside you, with no effort of your own, is 「<reading>たすかる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="助かる">to be saved / helped</vocabulary>.

tasukeru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="助">help</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="助ける">to help / rescue</vocabulary> word are the same. This ending points it outward, so you are the one reaching in and pulling someone else clear.
tasukeru.reading_mnemonic: You met this sound as たす in 助かる, so the outward version, <vocabulary form="助ける">to help / rescue</vocabulary>, is simply <reading>たすける</reading>.

tatoeba.meaning_mnemonic: To pin down what 'a bird' means you hold up one sparrow and one crow and let those two stand in for the whole idea. Reaching for a specific case to carry the general one is <vocabulary form="例えば">for example</vocabulary>.
tatoeba.reading_mnemonic: The artist at the <reading>tattoo bar</reading> never describes a style in words. She flips to one drawing, says <reading>たとえば</reading> this dragon, and lets that single sample do the defining, which is <vocabulary form="例えば">for example</vocabulary>.

tatsu-time.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="経">pass through</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="経つ">for time to pass</vocabulary> word are the same; the extra kana on the end just makes it something time does by itself.
tatsu-time.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail a hiker misses the last bus and <reading>tuts</reading> at his watch while the daylight fades. Each tut marks another minute <vocabulary form="経つ">passing</vocabulary> with nothing to fill it, and that slow drip is <reading>たつ</reading>.

tatsu-v.meaning_mnemonic: You already met the <kanji>stand</kanji> kanji, and the <vocabulary>to stand</vocabulary> word is that same character with nothing changed. The trailing kana just makes it something you do.
tatsu-v.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail a hiker's tent is so <reading>tatty</reading> it collapses flat the moment he lies down. With no floor left, he has to <vocabulary>stand</vocabulary> until sunrise, grumbling 「<reading>たつ</reading>」.

te-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>hand</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>hand</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so whatever one means, the other means too.
te-v.reading_mnemonic: A masseuse leans her whole weight through one <reading>tender</reading> <vocabulary>hand</vocabulary> pressed flat to your spine, and the tool doing the work is called 「<reading>て</reading>」.

tebukuro.meaning_mnemonic: A snug <kanji form="袋">sack</kanji> sewn to the shape of a <kanji form="手">hand</kanji>, with a separate slot for each finger, is one of a pair of <vocabulary form="手袋">gloves</vocabulary>.

teeburu.meaning_mnemonic: A carpenter nails a flat plank across four fence posts and calls the whole thing a <reading>table</reading>. The family eats every meal hunched around that plank, so the plank is the <vocabulary>table</vocabulary> they point at and name 「<reading>テーブル</reading>」.

tegami.meaning_mnemonic: You fill a sheet of <kanji>paper</kanji> with words in your own <kanji>hand</kanji>, then fold it up and mail it. What lands in the far mailbox is a <vocabulary>letter</vocabulary>.

teian.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="提">carry</kanji> a worked-out <kanji form="案">plan</kanji> in your hands to the meeting and lay it flat on the table for the room. Set out to be judged like that, it is a <vocabulary form="提案">proposal</vocabulary>.

teikyou-suru.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="提">carry</kanji> a tray of samples to a customer in your hands and <kanji form="供">offer</kanji> each one across to them; passing goods to someone like that is to <vocabulary form="提供する">provide</vocabulary>.

teinei.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>town</kanji> this <kanji>peaceful</kanji> stays that way only because every resident is <vocabulary>polite / careful</vocabulary> with the next. It is a な adjective, so な slots in ahead of the noun it describes.

teishutsu-suru.meaning_mnemonic: The finished report stays in your hands until you <kanji form="提">carry</kanji> it to the front desk and let it <kanji form="出">leave</kanji> your fingers onto the tray. Letting a document exit you and stay with the office is how you <vocabulary form="提出する">submit</vocabulary> it.

tekitou.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="適">suitable</kanji> pick is the one that <kanji form="当">hit</kanji>s the target dead center, and a pick that lands there is <vocabulary form="適当">appropriate</vocabulary>. It is a な adjective, so な sits before the noun it describes.
tekitou.description: In careful use 適当 means fitting or suitable. In casual speech it often means the opposite: something done at random, with little thought.

ten-in.meaning_mnemonic: A roadside <kanji>shop</kanji> so small it keeps just one <kanji>employee</kanji> behind the counter, and that person is the <vocabulary>shop clerk</vocabulary>.

tenisu.meaning_mnemonic: Two <reading>tenants</reading> on either side of a net argue over every bounce by whacking a ball back across it. That racket-swung quarrel is <vocabulary form="テニス">tennis</vocabulary>, <reading>テニス</reading>.

tenki.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Heaven</kanji> picks an <kanji>energy</kanji> level every morning. Whether it comes out sparking and stormy or flat and grey, that level is the <vocabulary>weather</vocabulary>.

terebi.meaning_mnemonic: The picture on that glowing box in the corner is always <reading>terrible</reading>, yet the whole family stares at it for hours. That hypnotic screen of bad shows is the <vocabulary>TV</vocabulary>, the box everyone calls the <reading>テレビ</reading>.

terebi-bangumi.meaning_mnemonic: A <vocabulary form="番組">TV program</vocabulary> is a single <kanji form="番">numbered turn</kanji> in the evening's run, <kanji form="組">braided</kanji> between the show before it and the show after so the night plays with no gap.

tesuto.meaning_mnemonic: Tess never revises, so the pop quiz lands, she panics, kicks the desk leg, and jams her <reading>Tess toe</reading>. Her yelp of <reading>テスト</reading> is the sound of every surprise <vocabulary>test</vocabulary>.

tetsudatte-kureru.meaning_mnemonic: Someone puts a <kanji form="手">hand</kanji> to your job and lets their own plans <kanji form="伝">go along</kanji> with your work instead. Doing that for you is to <vocabulary form="手伝ってくれる">help (me)</vocabulary>.

tetsudau.meaning_mnemonic: You put your own <kanji>hand</kanji> to someone else's job. Staying to <kanji>go along</kanji> with their work until it is done is to <vocabulary>help</vocabulary>.

tobu.meaning_mnemonic: Your feet push off and for one long second the air holds your whole weight. That hanging second is what it means to <vocabulary>fly / jump</vocabulary>.
tobu.reading_mnemonic: A ghost behind the vending machine on the mountain trail grabs your <reading>toe</reading> and shouts <reading>boo</reading>. You <vocabulary>fly / jump</vocabulary> a clear metre off the path, yelping <reading>とぶ</reading>.

todokederu.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="届">deliver</kanji> a completed form to the city office and let it <kanji form="出">leave</kanji> your hands for good; that is to <vocabulary form="届け出る">report</vocabulary> or file something officially.

todokeru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="届">deliver</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="届ける">to deliver</vocabulary> word are the same character with the same meaning. The ける ending makes it transitive, so now someone is carrying a parcel and handing it to you.
todokeru.reading_mnemonic: You already learned 「とど」 from 届く, this word's intransitive partner, so its transitive form is simply <reading>とどける</reading> for <vocabulary form="届ける">to deliver</vocabulary>.

todoku-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="届">reach</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="届く">to reach</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they mean the same thing. With く on the end it is intransitive, so the parcel arrives on its own with no one delivering it.
todoku-v.reading_mnemonic: A kid at the riverbank lets a paper boat go, then only watches as it drifts down and bumps <reading>to a dock</reading> on its own. That soft knock against the post is <reading>とどく</reading>, a thing that manages <vocabulary form="届く">to reach</vocabulary> its place with nobody carrying it.

toire.meaning_mnemonic: An undignified raccoon at the riverbank keeps zapping the shallows with a <reading>toy ray</reading> gun, and every hit floats a porcelain <vocabulary>toilet</vocabulary> up out of the water and off downstream. By dusk the river is nothing but 「<reading>トイレ</reading>」 all the way to the bend.

tokei.meaning_mnemonic: Back when the village told the <kanji>time</kanji> by the sun on the temple roof, someone built a pocket machine to <kanji>plot</kanji> the hours instead. That gadget is a <vocabulary>clock / watch</vocabulary>.
tokei.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>tokay</reading> gecko clings to the wall and barks once an hour, right on the hour. The whole house tells time by the lizard now and calls it their <reading>とけい</reading>, a living <vocabulary>clock / watch</vocabulary>.

tokeru.meaning_mnemonic: Drop a sugar cube into hot tea and stir once. It loses its edges, goes cloudy, and spreads through the water until it is gone, and that is what <vocabulary form="溶ける">to melt / dissolve</vocabulary> looks like.
tokeru.reading_mnemonic: A chocolate coin left on the sunny windowsill goes from a hard <reading>token</reading> to a brown smear across the paint by noon. Something firm turning soft and runny with nobody touching it is 「<reading>とける</reading>」, <vocabulary form="溶ける">to melt / dissolve</vocabulary>.

tokidoki.meaning_mnemonic: A single <kanji>time</kanji> here, another <kanji>time</kanji> there, with long stretches of nothing wedged between them, is what adds up to <vocabulary>sometimes</vocabulary>.
tokidoki.reading_mnemonic: Ask the riverbank ferryman for a lift and <reading>ときどき</reading> he gives a lazy <reading>okey-dokey</reading> and reaches for his pole. The rest of the time he just pretends not to hear, which is exactly what <vocabulary>sometimes</vocabulary> feels like.

tokoro.meaning_mnemonic: A hiker on the mountain trail keeps one photo taped inside his hat. It marks the exact <vocabulary>place</vocabulary> where the path forks to the vending machine, and missing the fork costs him an hour back down.
tokoro.reading_mnemonic: The old ferryman only ever rows people to one muddy <vocabulary>place</vocabulary> on the far bank. He <reading>took a row</reading> out to that same landing so many thousands of times that the spot is now simply 「<reading>ところ</reading>」.

tokorode.meaning_mnemonic: Mid-conversation on the highway, the driver <reading>took a road</reading> off to the right with no warning and opened a whole new subject. Swerving the talk onto another route is <reading>ところで</reading>, <vocabulary form="ところで">by the way</vocabulary>.

tokubetsu.meaning_mnemonic: One cow, held <kanji form="別">separate</kanji> from the market herd for the temple alone, is <kanji form="特">special</kanji>. That set-apart quality is what <vocabulary form="特別">special</vocabulary> means, and as a な adjective the word takes な before its noun.

tokui.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji form="得">Getting</kanji> the exact result your <kanji form="意">heart</kanji> aimed at, time after time, is what being <vocabulary form="得意">good at</vocabulary> something feels like. It is a な adjective, so it takes な before the noun it describes.

tokuni.meaning_mnemonic: Pick one thing out of the herd and treat it as <kanji form="特">special</kanji>, the way the temple keeps a single cow that is never for eating. Marking that one out from all the rest is <vocabulary form="特に">especially</vocabulary>.

tomaru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>stop</kanji> kanji and the word <vocabulary>to stop</vocabulary> are the same character, so the meaning carries over. The trailing kana marks the intransitive one: something halts on its own, with nobody stopping it.
tomaru.reading_mnemonic: Toto the door-to-door turtle rolls a <reading>tomato</reading> off his shell and it wobbles to rest against a stone. The instant it 「<reading>とまる</reading>」, dead still, is something <vocabulary>stopping</vocabulary> on its own.

tomaru-stay.meaning_mnemonic: Night drops on the mountain trail before you clear the ridge, and going down blind is how people get hurt. You take the bunk in the trail hut, boots by the door, and <vocabulary>stay overnight</vocabulary>.
tomaru-stay.reading_mnemonic: A traveler misses the last train and the innkeeper waves her in: there is a spare room, sort it out <reading>tomorrow</reading>. Sleeping the night somewhere that is not your own home is 「<reading>とまる</reading>」, <vocabulary>to stay overnight</vocabulary>.

tomeru-stop.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>stop</kanji> kanji and the word <vocabulary>to stop</vocabulary> are the same character, meaning unchanged. The trailing kana make it the transitive one: you bring something else to a halt, it does not halt itself.
tomeru-stop.reading_mnemonic: You already know this reading of 止 from 止まる, so when it is you bringing something else to a halt, <vocabulary>to stop</vocabulary> it is <reading>とめる</reading>.

tomodachi.meaning_mnemonic: Two hands closing together as a <kanji>friend</kanji> finally <kanji>reach</kanji> each other, and that arrival is what makes a <vocabulary>friend</vocabulary>.

tonari.meaning_mnemonic: The house sharing your wall is so close you hear its radio through the plaster and its cat scratches at your door. That wall-to-wall closeness is your <vocabulary>neighbor</vocabulary>.
tonari.reading_mnemonic: In the shop <vocabulary>next to</vocabulary> Koichi's, a ferret grabs a tuna-on-rye off the counter and bolts through a gap in the fence. A <reading>tuna rye</reading> lifted from one door over is <reading>となり</reading>.

too.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>ten</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>ten things</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so counting up to ten is all this one ever means.
too.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini he stubs his <reading>toe</reading> on the shelf ten times, yelping <reading>とお</reading> each time, and swears the broken onigiri come to exactly <vocabulary>ten things</vocabulary>.

tooi.meaning_mnemonic: From the top of the mountain trail, Koichi's konbini is one bright dot you can hide behind your thumb. Only real distance shrinks a shop like that, so it must be <vocabulary>far</vocabulary>.
tooi.reading_mnemonic: A barefoot hiker on the mountain trail lifts one <reading>toe</reading> and it completely blots out the vending machine at the summit. Anything a bare toe can blot out has to be <reading>とおい</reading>, plain <vocabulary>far</vocabulary>.

tooka.meaning_mnemonic: Count out <kanji>ten</kanji> full <kanji>days</kanji> on the calendar and the square you land on is the <vocabulary>10th / ten days</vocabulary>.

tooru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="通">traffic</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="通る">to pass through</vocabulary> word are the same word. With this ending it just means something moves along the road and out the far side on its own, with nobody pushing it.
tooru.reading_mnemonic: The <reading>toll</reading>-gate guard lifts the barrier for one more truck and it rolls straight past him into the dark. A thing that goes in one side of a gap and out the far side on its own is 「<reading>とおる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="通る">to pass through</vocabulary>.

toosu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="通">traffic</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="通す">to let pass</vocabulary> word are the same. This ending adds a hand on the gate, so someone now moves the traffic through instead of it flowing past on its own.
toosu.reading_mnemonic: You already know 通 sounds like とお from 通る, so the hands-on version, <vocabulary form="通す">to let pass</vocabulary>, is just <reading>とおす</reading>.

toranpu.meaning_mnemonic: In a game of whist the one suit that beats all the others is the <reading>trump</reading>, and the full deck you deal it from is <vocabulary form="トランプ">playing cards</vocabulary>, <reading>トランプ</reading>.

tori.meaning_mnemonic: Anything that can sit on a branch, let go, and still not fall is a <vocabulary>bird</vocabulary>.
tori.reading_mnemonic: Something swoops onto the mountain trail vending machine, rips open a snack bag, and is gone before the hiker turns around. He just sighs 「<reading>とり</reading>」, like the word <reading>tore</reading>, because the little robber that shredded his snack is a <vocabulary>bird</vocabulary>.

torihiki.meaning_mnemonic: Every time a shopkeeper lets you <kanji form="引">pull</kanji> goods across the counter and <kanji form="取">take</kanji> them while your cash slides the other way, that swap is a <vocabulary form="取引">transaction</vocabulary>.
torihiki.reading_mnemonic: Toto the door-to-door turtle settles every <vocabulary form="取引">transaction</vocabulary> with a quick round of <reading>Tori hockey</reading>, whacking a bottle cap across the counter to the buyer. Win or lose, the deal is closed, and that game is <reading>とりひき</reading>.

torihikisaki.meaning_mnemonic: The outside firm you <kanji form="取">take</kanji> orders from and <kanji form="引">pull</kanji> deals back and forth with, always one step <kanji form="先">ahead</kanji> of you along the trade line, is your <vocabulary form="取引先">business partner/client</vocabulary>.
torihikisaki.reading_mnemonic: Toto the door-to-door turtle trips on a shop's step and <reading>tears a hockey sack</reading> of samples over their floor. They forgive him and reorder for years, so that shop stays Toto's loyal <vocabulary form="取引先">business partner/client</vocabulary>, his 「<reading>とりひきさき</reading>」.

torikaeru.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="取">take</kanji> the worn part out by the ear, the rude fast way, and drop a fresh one into the gap it left. Swapping the old for the new like that is <vocabulary form="取り替える">to exchange / replace</vocabulary>.

torikakaru.meaning_mnemonic: You get a grip on the job and <kanji form="掛">hang</kanji> your whole weight from it, the rude fast way you would <kanji form="取">take</kanji> hold of someone by the ear. Latching on and leaning in like that is <vocabulary form="取り掛かる">to set about (a task)</vocabulary>.

toru.meaning_mnemonic: Reach out, close your hand on something that was not yours a second ago, and pull it back to your chest. That motion, from start to finish, is what it means to <vocabulary>take</vocabulary>.
toru.reading_mnemonic: A magpie drops onto the picnic table, clamps its beak on your last rice ball, and is airborne before you flinch. It <reading>tore</reading> the food straight out of your hand, and to <vocabulary>grab</vocabulary> is <reading>とる</reading>.

toshi-city.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="都">metropolis</kanji> built up by constant new arrivals, with a <kanji form="市">market</kanji> square beating at its center, is a <vocabulary form="都市">city (urban)</vocabulary>.

toshokan.meaning_mnemonic: Pack a <kanji>building</kanji> with every <kanji>map</kanji> ever folded and everything a brush could <kanji>write</kanji>, and you have a <vocabulary>library</vocabulary>.

totemo.meaning_mnemonic: The <reading>totem</reading> pole at the shrine gate is carved so absurdly tall its top face vanishes into cloud, the village's way of saying these spirits are <reading>とても</reading> — <vocabulary>very</vocabulary> — important.

touji.meaning_mnemonic: Point back at a past event and name the exact <kanji form="時">hour</kanji> it happened. The moment your finger <kanji form="当">hit</kanji>s is what people call <vocabulary form="当時">at that time</vocabulary>.

touzen.meaning_mnemonic: An answer that <kanji form="当">hit</kanji>s exactly what everyone already expected needs no defending; it is <vocabulary form="当然">naturally</vocabulary> right. Being a な adjective, it takes な before the noun it describes.

tsugi.meaning_mnemonic: The deli counter light clicks from one number straight to the number right after it. Whoever is holding that ticket is <vocabulary>next</vocabulary>.
tsugi.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank a <reading>tugboat</reading> shoves each moored barge aside so the one behind it can slide into the dock. Its horn blasts <reading>つぎ</reading> for the <vocabulary>next</vocabulary> boat in line.

tsugou.meaning_mnemonic: Lay <kanji>all</kanji> of your commitments in a row and check whether a new plan will <kanji>fit</kanji> among them. How easily it fits is its <vocabulary>convenience</vocabulary>.

tsuini.meaning_mnemonic: Six hours up the mountain trail, the hiker reaches the top and drops <reading>to a knee</reading> by the vending machine. He is <reading>ついに</reading> done, and arriving after everything like that is <vocabulary form="ついに">finally / at last</vocabulary>.

tsuitachi.meaning_mnemonic: The flat line of <kanji>one</kanji> sits right against the <kanji>day</kanji> mark on the calendar. That opening pair is always the <vocabulary>1st of the month</vocabulary>.
tsuitachi.reading_mnemonic: Every <reading>ついたち</reading>, landlord <reading>Sweetie Tachi</reading> pounds on the door, because rent is only ever due on the <vocabulary>1st of the month</vocabulary>.

tsukaeru.meaning_mnemonic: Nothing new happens here: the <kanji form="使">use</kanji> kanji you already know is exactly what <vocabulary form="使える">can use</vocabulary> means.
tsukaeru.reading_mnemonic: You already met 「つか」 in 使う, so <vocabulary form="使える">can use</vocabulary> just wears that same reading with a new tail: <reading>つかえる</reading>.

tsukau.meaning_mnemonic: The lone vending machine on the mountain trail is there for one purpose. Feeding it a coin and pressing the button is what it means <vocabulary>to use</vocabulary> it.
tsukau.reading_mnemonic: The trail farmer keeps <reading>two cows</reading> yoked behind the vending machine. When a snack jams, driving the pair in as a battering ram is all anyone has <vocabulary>to use</vocabulary> <reading>つかう</reading> up here.

tsukeru.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini a customer will <reading>tuck a roo</reading> toy under one arm, clip its leash to a bag strap, and thumb its light-up eyes on in a single move. One motion that both fastens a thing and powers it up is <vocabulary>to turn on / attach</vocabulary> it, <reading>つける</reading>.

tsuki-v.meaning_mnemonic: You already carry this character as the <kanji>moon</kanji> kanji, and the <vocabulary>moon</vocabulary> word asks nothing more of it: same shape, same meaning.
tsuki-v.reading_mnemonic: The cats at Grandma Kane's shrine line up on the mossy steps each clear night to watch one pale disc slide overhead. Grandma calls it 「<reading>つき</reading>」, like <reading>ski</reading>, and that disc the cats never look away from is the <vocabulary>moon</vocabulary>.

tsukue.meaning_mnemonic: Shove a plain table into the corner and aim a lamp at it, and now people only sit there to write, never to eat. A table you work at instead of dine at is a <vocabulary>desk</vocabulary>.
tsukue.reading_mnemonic: A pigeon wanders into Sei's school, heads straight for the one flat surface with drawers and a lamp, and settles down <reading>to coo, eh</reading>. The writing table it picked is a <vocabulary>desk</vocabulary>, and it has left feathers all across the <reading>つくえ</reading>.

tsukuru.meaning_mnemonic: A crew at the riverbank ties loose reeds together until the heap becomes a raft that floats. Turning scattered junk into a thing that was not there an hour ago is <vocabulary>to make</vocabulary> it.
tsukuru.reading_mnemonic: The riverbank boatwright never works alone. They <reading>took a crew</reading> of two, because <vocabulary>to make</vocabulary> <reading>つくる</reading> a whole canoe alone in one day is impossible.

tsukutte-ageru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="作">make</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="作ってあげる">to make (for someone)</vocabulary> word are the same word, so at heart it just means make. The tail on the end only adds that you make the thing for someone else, not for yourself.
tsukutte-ageru.reading_mnemonic: You already know 作 is 「つく」 from 作る, the verb it first appeared in, so <vocabulary form="作ってあげる">to make (for someone)</vocabulary> is <reading>つくってあげる</reading>.

tsuma.meaning_mnemonic: The person who knows exactly where every spare key in the house is hidden is your <vocabulary>wife</vocabulary>.
tsuma.reading_mnemonic: The family dog barks <reading>つま</reading> every time the door opens. It sounds just like <reading>too-mah</reading>, which is somehow always right when your <vocabulary>wife</vocabulary> walks in.

tsumaranai.meaning_mnemonic: A museum audio guide has one narrator with one flat tone, sighing <reading>'Sue, ma, run, aye'</reading> at every single painting. Forty rooms of that drone is <vocabulary>boring</vocabulary> boiled down, and <reading>つまらない</reading> is the sound the sigh already makes.

tsumari.meaning_mnemonic: At the end of class the teacher wipes the board and writes one short line under everything that was there. Boiling the whole hour down to that single <reading>summary</reading> is <reading>つまり</reading>, <vocabulary form="つまり">in other words</vocabulary>.

tsumetai.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>chill</kanji> in this word has soaked into a thing rather than the air. Touch a soda can, a metal railing, or a hand you shake outdoors in winter, and what your skin reports is <vocabulary>cold (to touch)</vocabulary>.
tsumetai.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a clerk named <reading>Tai</reading> reaches into the freezer and yanks his hand straight back, hissing. Every can down there is <reading>つめたい</reading> enough to sting bare skin, and that bite is pure <vocabulary>cold (to touch)</vocabulary>.

tsuredeiku.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="行">go</kanji> off down the crossroads with your little brother gripped by the sleeve so he cannot peel away. Setting out with a person fastened to your side like that is <vocabulary form="連れて行く">to take (a person) along</vocabulary>.

tsuretekuru.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="連">lead</kanji> a nervous friend up the path by the hand as the two of you <kanji form="来">come</kanji> toward the house. Turning up with an extra person beside you is <vocabulary form="連れて来る">to bring (a person)</vocabulary>.

tsuri.meaning_mnemonic: Sit on the riverbank, bait a hook, and drop it on a long line into the water. Waiting like that for something below to pull is <vocabulary form="釣り">fishing</vocabulary>.
tsuri.reading_mnemonic: You already met this sound as 「つ」 in お釣り, the change handed back at a shop, so the word for <vocabulary form="釣り">fishing</vocabulary> is just <reading>つり</reading>.

tsutaeru.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>walk along</kanji> a message, carrying it down a line of people one hand to the next, until it reaches the far end. Passing something all the way down the line is what it means <vocabulary>to convey / tell</vocabulary>.
tsutaeru.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>two-tailer</reading> lizard courier sprints between houses, flicking one tail per word so the next house gets the message. A tail-flicked relay like that is what it means <vocabulary>to convey / tell</vocabulary>, and its name is 「<reading>つたえる</reading>」.

tsutawaru.meaning_mnemonic: A message that will <kanji form="伝">go along</kanji> by itself, passed from mouth to mouth with no one carrying it, is one that comes <vocabulary form="伝わる">to be conveyed</vocabulary>.
tsutawaru.reading_mnemonic: You already know 伝 is 「つた」 from 伝える, so for a word <vocabulary form="伝わる">to be conveyed</vocabulary> across a crowd is <reading>つたわる</reading>.

tsuyoi.meaning_mnemonic: At the school sports day, one first-year on the tug-of-war rope drags the entire opposing team over the line by herself. Being able to move people who refuse to move is <vocabulary>strong</vocabulary>.
tsuyoi.reading_mnemonic: A swamped rowboat slides off down the river until Sue wades in and drags it up the bank alone, the ferryman shouting <reading>'Sue, oi'</reading> after her. Hauling a full boat against the current is <reading>つよい</reading>, plain <vocabulary>strong</vocabulary>.

tsuzukeru-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="続">continue</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="続ける">to continue</vocabulary> word are the same word. This is the form with a hand on the spool, someone pulling more thread off on purpose.
tsuzukeru-v.reading_mnemonic: You already know 続 is 「つづ」 from 続き, so for a worker <vocabulary form="続ける">to continue</vocabulary> a task without a break is <reading>つづける</reading>.

tsuzuki.meaning_mnemonic: The stretch where something that <kanji>continues</kanji> picks up again, right after it looked finished, is its <vocabulary>continuation</vocabulary>.
tsuzuki.reading_mnemonic: Sue the zookeeper never lets a tour end. She jangles her <reading>zoo key</reading>, and 「<reading>つづき</reading>」 unlocks one more gate into the <vocabulary>continuation</vocabulary>.

tsuzuku.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="続">continue</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="続く">to continue</vocabulary> word are the same word. This is the form that runs on by itself, the thread unrolling off the spool with no one feeding it.
tsuzuku.reading_mnemonic: You already know 続 is 「つづ」 from 続き, so for a spell of good weather <vocabulary form="続く">to continue</vocabulary> on its own is <reading>つづく</reading>.

uchi.meaning_mnemonic: Trip over the cat, howl <reading>ouch</reading>, and the one place nobody outside your circle hears you do it is <reading>うち</reading>, your <vocabulary>home</vocabulary> and everyone inside it.

udon.meaning_mnemonic: The chef barks that <reading>you don't</reading> ever roll these noodles thin, and slaps out a fat white rope of dough. That thick noodle is <vocabulary form="うどん">udon noodles</vocabulary>, <reading>うどん</reading>.

ue.meaning_mnemonic: Standing by itself, the <kanji>up</kanji> kanji is just the <vocabulary>up</vocabulary> word, nothing added.
ue.reading_mnemonic: A monkey named Louie has stranded his chocolate bar on top of the summit vending machine and cannot reach it. He just points <vocabulary>up</vocabulary> and wails his own name: <reading>Louie</reading>, <reading>うえ</reading>.

ugokasu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>move</kanji> kanji and the word <vocabulary>to move</vocabulary> are the same character, meaning unchanged. The かす ending makes it the transitive one: you are the one shoving something else into motion.
ugokasu.reading_mnemonic: You already know this reading of 動 from 動く, so when you are the one making something else move, <vocabulary>to move</vocabulary> it, the word is <reading>うごかす</reading>.

ugoku.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>move</kanji> kanji and the word <vocabulary>to move</vocabulary> are the same character, so the meaning carries over. The trailing kana mark the intransitive one: the thing shifts on its own, with nobody pushing it.
ugoku.reading_mnemonic: Sei leans on a stalled merry-go-round, mutters <reading>you go, cuckoo</reading>, and it lurches into a slow spin on its own, 「<reading>うごく</reading>」, that first shift from dead still being what it means to <vocabulary>move</vocabulary>.

ukabu.meaning_mnemonic: You let go of the beach ball under the pool water and it shoots straight back up to sit on the surface. A thing riding on top of the water instead of going under is what it is to <vocabulary form="浮かぶ">float</vocabulary>.
ukabu.reading_mnemonic: You <reading>hook a boot</reading> out of the canal, and it will not stay under no matter how you shove it. It keeps riding back up to the top, and sitting on the surface like that is what it means to <vocabulary form="浮かぶ">float</vocabulary>, 「<reading>うかぶ</reading>」.

ukagau.meaning_mnemonic: You knock softly and wait outside the doorway until someone waves you in, then lean your head through to put your question. Approaching a person's home and their attention that carefully is to <vocabulary form="伺う">visit and ask humbly</vocabulary>.
ukagau.reading_mnemonic: A polite <reading>kangaroo</reading> props its paws on the garden fence and waits to be waved through before hopping in to ask after your health. Peeking in and raising a question that gently is <vocabulary form="伺う">to visit and ask humbly</vocabulary>, which comes out as <reading>うかがう</reading>.

uketsuke.meaning_mnemonic: The first desk inside the door <kanji form="受">accepts</kanji> your name and <kanji form="付">attaches</kanji> you to the person you came to see. That desk is the <vocabulary form="受付">reception (desk)</vocabulary>.
uketsuke.reading_mnemonic: A bowing front-desk clerk greets every visitor with the same line: 「OK, <reading>take a key</reading>.」 Blur those words together and you hear <reading>うけつけ</reading>, the <vocabulary form="受付">reception (desk)</vocabulary> where everyone checks in.

uma.meaning_mnemonic: The animal that walks over to the paddock fence stands taller than you at the shoulder, long-faced, with a mane down its neck and a sweeping tail. That shape and size is a <vocabulary form="馬">horse</vocabulary>.
uma.reading_mnemonic: A toddler on the trail points at the animal being led past and gasps <reading>ooh, ma</reading> at her mother. The thing she means is a <vocabulary form="馬">horse</vocabulary>, and the word she wants is 「<reading>うま</reading>」.

umareru.meaning_mnemonic: A brand-new <kanji>life</kanji> that was nowhere a minute ago and is suddenly here, breathing on its own. That sudden arrival is what it means to <vocabulary>be born</vocabulary>.
umareru.reading_mnemonic: A stray <reading>mare</reading> wanders onto the school sports field at dawn and drops her foal in the wet grass with no fuss at all. Watching it stagger upright is watching something <vocabulary>be born</vocabulary>, and she nickers a low 「<reading>うまれる</reading>」 over it.

umi.meaning_mnemonic: The one thing wide enough that you cannot see the far side, deep enough that nothing you drop comes back, and salty enough to sting a cut is the <vocabulary>sea</vocabulary>.
umi.reading_mnemonic: A sailor steps off the last dock, sees nothing but water clear to the horizon, thumps his chest and booms 「<reading>うみ</reading>」, like <reading>ooh, me</reading>. All that flat endless salt water in front of him is the <vocabulary>sea</vocabulary>.

undou-suru.meaning_mnemonic: What it means <vocabulary form="運動する">to exercise</vocabulary> is to <kanji form="運">carry</kanji> your own body through enough hard <kanji form="動">motion</kanji> to leave you breathless.

unten-suru.meaning_mnemonic: Give the wheels that only <kanji>revolve</kanji> some real road to bite, and the spin finally <kanji>carries</kanji> the whole car forward. Sitting up front making that happen is what it means <vocabulary>to drive</vocabulary>.

urayamashii.meaning_mnemonic: Your friend shows you her new apartment with the huge balcony and the view of the park, and yours looks at a wall. That hot, sour wish to have her place instead of yours is being <vocabulary form="羨ましい">envious</vocabulary>.
urayamashii.reading_mnemonic: From the station platform you watch a neighbour slide into a low red car while you wait for the last train. You groan 「<reading>うらやましい</reading>」, because <reading>you're a Maserati</reading> owner and you are not, and that ache is being <vocabulary form="羨ましい">envious</vocabulary>.

ureshii.meaning_mnemonic: A dog hears the leash come off its hook and understands a walk is coming. The whole body wags at once, and that full-body wag is <vocabulary>happy / glad</vocabulary>.
ureshii.reading_mnemonic: Reiko finds one last scoop of <reading>relish</reading> in the jar and does a little hop. Hear <reading>うれしい</reading> as that relish-hop and you have <vocabulary>happy / glad</vocabulary>.

uriage.meaning_mnemonic: Each time you <kanji form="売">sell</kanji> something the price adds <kanji form="上">up</kanji> onto the day's running total, and that whole pile of takings is the <vocabulary form="売上">sales (revenue)</vocabulary>.
uriage.reading_mnemonic: Uri's fruit stall makes all its money through one till, so she reads that machine like <reading>a gauge</reading> of the whole month. The total it rings up is the stall's <vocabulary form="売上">sales (revenue)</vocabulary>, the figure she means when she says 「<reading>うりあげ</reading>」.

uriba.meaning_mnemonic: The lit patch of <kanji form="場">place</kanji> on a shop floor where the staff do nothing but <kanji form="売">sell</kanji> one kind of goods is that department's <vocabulary form="売り場">sales floor</vocabulary>.

uru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>sell</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to sell</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
uru.reading_mnemonic: A snail runs a little stall on the mossy shrine steps and passes trinkets to the cats one at a time. Every sale leaves a shiny <reading>ooze</reading> trail on the stone, so <reading>うる</reading> means <vocabulary>to sell</vocabulary>.

ushi.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="牛">cow</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="牛">cow</vocabulary> word are exactly the same character, so they mean the same thing.
ushi.reading_mnemonic: The dairy farmer leans on the gate watching his best milker chew and sighs that <reading>ooh, she</reading> is a fine one. The animal he means is a <vocabulary form="牛">cow</vocabulary>, and he calls her 「<reading>うし</reading>」.

ushiro.meaning_mnemonic: This word is just the <kanji>behind</kanji> kanji you already know, so <vocabulary>behind</vocabulary> is exactly what it means.
ushiro.reading_mnemonic: A duck on the riverbank rowed so hard she left the whole regatta <vocabulary>behind</vocabulary> her. Watch her wake and you still hear it: <reading>she rowed</reading>, <reading>うしろ</reading>.

uta.meaning_mnemonic: Words turn into a <vocabulary>song</vocabulary> the moment a tune picks them up and makes them rise and fall instead of lying flat.
uta.reading_mnemonic: You already met this reading in 歌う, so a <vocabulary>song</vocabulary> is just <reading>うた</reading> again.

utau.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>song</kanji> sits silent on the page until a voice lifts it into the air. Pushing it out of your mouth like that is what it means to <vocabulary>sing</vocabulary>.
utau.reading_mnemonic: Every dawn a cat squeezes inside the shrine's great bell and belts a long note that ends on a proud <reading>you-ta-daa</reading>. The bell booms it back doubled, and that racket is the cat's idea of how to 「<reading>うたう</reading>」 and <vocabulary>sing</vocabulary>.

wafuu.meaning_mnemonic: You already know <kanji form="和">harmony</kanji> also stands for Japan itself, and <kanji form="風">wind</kanji> can mean the air or manner of a thing. So the Japanese manner of doing something is <vocabulary form="和風">Japanese-style</vocabulary>.

wagamama.meaning_mnemonic: A <reading>wagon mama</reading> drags the family cart to whatever shop she fancies and never asks where anyone else wants to go. Putting your own way ahead of everyone else's is <vocabulary form="わがまま">selfish</vocabulary>, and that pushy <reading>わがまま</reading> sound carries the same trait.

wain.meaning_mnemonic: A small child at the table starts to <reading>whine</reading> the moment the adults uncork the dark red bottle and fill their glasses. That guarded grown-up drink is <reading>ワイン</reading>, the <vocabulary form="ワイン">wine</vocabulary>.

wakai.meaning_mnemonic: At the shrine, Grandma Kane swears she is still <vocabulary>young</vocabulary> as she chases the cats up the mossy steps two at a time. The い on the end is the marker that makes it an adjective, free to sit before any noun.
wakai.reading_mnemonic: A wacky teenager grinds their skateboard down the school's echoing hallway, shouting that only the <vocabulary>young</vocabulary> would try a stunt this <reading>wacky</reading>. The boast stuck, and now everyone says <reading>わかい</reading>.

wakaru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>understand</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to understand</vocabulary> word are the same character, so the meaning carries straight over. The kana tacked on the end makes it a verb that just happens on its own.
wakaru.reading_mnemonic: A fisher on the riverbank stares at a tangled line until, all at once, the whole knot resolves in her head and she blurts 「<reading>わかる</reading>」. The cry lands right on <reading>wah-kah-roo</reading>, the sound of a thing you finally <vocabulary>understand</vocabulary>.

wakasu.meaning_mnemonic: You stand over the pot with the gas turned up full, holding the water on the heat until it roars. Driving water up to a rolling churn yourself is what it is to <vocabulary form="沸かす">boil</vocabulary> it.
wakasu.reading_mnemonic: You already know this sound from 沸く, so the twin where you are the one heating the water up to a churn is <reading>わかす</reading>, to <vocabulary form="沸かす">boil</vocabulary> it.

waku.meaning_mnemonic: You set the kettle on a high flame and wait until the surface is rolling over and throwing off steam. Water climbing to that churn on its own is what it is to <vocabulary form="沸く">boil</vocabulary>.
waku.reading_mnemonic: Koichi fills a steel <reading>wok</reading> with water on the konbini hotplate, and soon it is heaving and spitting all by itself. Water going wild with heat like that is what it means to <vocabulary form="沸く">boil</vocabulary>, 「<reading>わく</reading>」.

warau.meaning_mnemonic: Your mouth pulls wide, your cheeks bunch up under your eyes, and air comes out of you in short barks you cannot hold back. That whole helpless reaction is what it means to <vocabulary>laugh / smile</vocabulary>.
warau.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>walrus</reading> hauls out on the riverbank, flops flat into the mud, and lies there with both flippers up, hugely pleased with itself. You take one look and <vocabulary>laugh / smile</vocabulary>, and its wet, satisfied rumble comes out as 「<reading>わらう</reading>」.

waribiki.meaning_mnemonic: Cut the price into equal <kanji form="割">proportion</kanji>s, then <kanji form="引">pull</kanji> a few of those parts away before you pay. The parts pulled off the total are the <vocabulary form="割引">discount</vocabulary>.
waribiki.reading_mnemonic: Wally jabs a <reading>wobbly key</reading> into the till and springs the drawer open. He counts cash back into your hand off the price you owed, and that money handed back is a <reading>わりびき</reading>, a <vocabulary form="割引">discount</vocabulary>.

warui.meaning_mnemonic: Whatever noun you set this in front of, it drags the thing down. The い hanging off the end makes it an adjective, and the verdict it lands on is <vocabulary>bad</vocabulary>.
warui.reading_mnemonic: Every time the puppy Rooey chews through another shoe, his owner throws up her hands and groans <reading>wah, Rooey</reading>. That groan is 「<reading>わるい</reading>」, and it means the dog has been <vocabulary>bad</vocabulary>.

washoku.meaning_mnemonic: Take that same <kanji form="和">harmony</kanji> that also stands for Japan, set it in front of <kanji form="食">food</kanji>, and you have the home-side cooking of rice, fish and miso that is <vocabulary form="和食">Japanese food</vocabulary>.

wasureru.meaning_mnemonic: You set your keys down somewhere so ordinary your brain never files it, and an hour later that spot is a blank. Letting a thing fall clean out of your head is to <vocabulary>forget</vocabulary> it.
wasureru.reading_mnemonic: Koichi swore he <reading>was surely</reading> saving you the last onigiri, then sold it to the next customer, the promise gone from his head. That clean drop out of mind is to <vocabulary>forget</vocabulary>, and its sound is <reading>わすれる</reading>.

watar.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>ford</kanji> the shallow river stepping stone by stepping stone until you reach the far bank. Getting all the way to the other side is what it means to <vocabulary>cross</vocabulary>.
watar.reading_mnemonic: Each step the heron takes through the <reading>water</reading> makes a slow suck and slap, 「<reading>わたる</reading>」, as it works toward the other side. That patient wade is the bird choosing to <vocabulary>cross</vocabulary>.

watashi.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>private</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>I / me</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
watashi.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a hoarder snatches the last piece of sushi and snaps <reading>わたし</reading>, which sounds just like <reading>what a sushi</reading>, because only <vocabulary>me</vocabulary> gets to eat it.

watashitachi.meaning_mnemonic: Each <kanji>private</kanji> stash belongs to one person, but stand a whole row of them side by side and that row becomes <vocabulary>we</vocabulary>.
watashitachi.reading_mnemonic: You already know 私 reads わたし, so adding たち turns <vocabulary>we</vocabulary> into <reading>わたしたち</reading>.

watasu.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>ferry</kanji> the parcel across the last stretch of counter. Passing it into the customer's open hands is to <vocabulary>hand it over</vocabulary>.
watasu.reading_mnemonic: You already know 渡 from 渡る, where it means getting across, so passing a thing all the way into another hand, <vocabulary>to hand over</vocabulary>, is <reading>わたす</reading>.

wazato.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine one cat <reading>waltzed to</reading> the bell rope, smooth and unhurried, and hauled it down. A walk that deliberate proves the cat rang the bell <reading>わざと</reading>, that is, <vocabulary form="わざと">on purpose</vocabulary>.

wazawaza.meaning_mnemonic: Sei steps off the fairground <reading>waltzer, waltzer</reading> and walks straight back to the end of the queue for another turn. Riding the very same thing twice on purpose is <reading>わざわざ</reading>, <vocabulary form="わざわざ">specially / deliberately</vocabulary>.

yagate.meaning_mnemonic: An hour down the lane, <reading>a gate</reading> comes into view up ahead. Reaching it will happen <reading>やがて</reading>, which is <vocabulary form="やがて">soon / before long</vocabulary>.

yahari.meaning_mnemonic: The offering bowl at Grandma Kane's shrine is tipped over again, and <reading>yeah, Harry</reading> the fat tom cat is sitting right beside it. It went the way everyone knew it would, and that is <reading>やはり</reading>, <vocabulary form="やはり">as expected / after all</vocabulary>.

yakkyoku.meaning_mnemonic: The one <kanji>office</kanji> licensed to weigh out <kanji>medicine</kanji> brewed from bitter grass is a <vocabulary>pharmacy</vocabulary>.

yakusoku.meaning_mnemonic: A <vocabulary>promise / appointment</vocabulary> is a <kanji>bundle</kanji> of your own future hours. You tie it shut and hand it to someone else to hold.

yakyuu.meaning_mnemonic: Take the open <kanji form="野">field</kanji> the village never fenced, add one hard <kanji form="球">ball</kanji> and nine leather gloves, and the game they play out there is <vocabulary form="野球">baseball</vocabulary>.

yama-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>mountain</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>mountain</vocabulary> word are the same character start to finish, so you already know everything it means.
yama-v.reading_mnemonic: At the petting-zoo hill a stubborn llama plants its feet halfway up and brays 「<reading>やま</reading>」 at the summit, a sound like <reading>llama</reading> itself. The big rock it flatly refuses to climb is a <vocabulary>mountain</vocabulary>.

yappari.meaning_mnemonic: The dog tied outside Koichi's konbini barks the second the door chime sounds, a flat <reading>yap already</reading>, right on cue like every other day. Calling that no-surprise-there in a casual voice is <reading>やっぱり</reading>, <vocabulary form="やっぱり">as expected (casual)</vocabulary>.

yaraseru.meaning_mnemonic: Run a <reading>yard sale</reading> and you get one afternoon to <vocabulary form="やらせる">make or let someone else do</vocabulary> every bit of the lifting and pricing. Handing the whole driveway to other hands like that is <reading>やらせる</reading>.

yarinaosu.meaning_mnemonic: The moment the work goes wrong, you <kanji form="直">straightaway</kanji> tear it down and carry the pieces back to step one. Building it again from the start like that is <vocabulary form="やり直す">to redo / start over</vocabulary>.
yarinaosu.reading_mnemonic: You already know 直 is 「なお」 from 直す, the verb it first appeared in, so <vocabulary form="やり直す">to redo / start over</vocabulary> is <reading>やりなおす</reading>.

yasai.meaning_mnemonic: Green things that come up on their own out on the untended <kanji>plains</kanji>, with no farmer and no fence, still get gathered up and eaten as <vocabulary>vegetables</vocabulary>.

yasai-itame.meaning_mnemonic: Take <kanji form="菜">greens</kanji> pulled straight from the open <kanji form="野">field</kanji>, throw them into a scorching pan and <kanji form="炒">roast</kanji> them fast, and you have <vocabulary form="野菜炒め">stir-fried vegetables</vocabulary>.

yasashii.meaning_mnemonic: Today's test at the school is a single question asking whether the sky is above you or below you. Sei circles 'above' without sitting down, because a test that answers itself is <vocabulary>easy</vocabulary>.
yasashii.reading_mnemonic: A new kid at the school meets every hard question from the teacher with a shrug and a mellow <reading>yeah, sushi</reading>. Nothing rattles him, so his whole week feels <reading>やさしい</reading>, which is to say <vocabulary>easy</vocabulary>.

yasashii-n4.meaning_mnemonic: A person who meets everyone with <kanji form="優">tenderness</kanji>, quick to go easy on you and slow to judge, is what Japanese calls <vocabulary form="優しい">kind / gentle</vocabulary>. The final い is the ending that makes it an adjective.
yasashii-n4.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine the old woman presses a warm tray of sushi into the hands of every cold visitor and asks for nothing back. People say 「<reading>やさしい</reading>」 as they eat, because a <reading>yeah, sushi</reading> welcome that open is exactly <vocabulary form="優しい">kind / gentle</vocabulary>.

yasui-adj.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>cheap</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>cheap</vocabulary> word are one and the same, so they mean the same thing. That final い is what turns it into an adjective, a marker every い adjective shares.
yasui-adj.reading_mnemonic: A farmer loads his cart with <vocabulary>cheap</vocabulary> bruised apples, so pleased with the price that he calls his pig over with a cheerful <reading>“ya, sooey!”</reading>, which is just <reading>やすい</reading>.

yasumu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>rest</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to rest</vocabulary> word are the same character carrying the same meaning. The kana on the tail is only there so you can conjugate it like a verb.
yasumu.reading_mnemonic: Halfway through his shift, Koichi yawns so hard the till blurs, and he answers a customer with a dozy <reading>'yes, mum'</reading>. He shuts the register and decides to <vocabulary>rest</vocabulary> for what is left of the day, yawning 「<reading>やすむ</reading>」.

yatte-ageru.meaning_mnemonic: Out on the <reading>yacht, a giraffe</reading> leans up and knots the top sail no sailor can reach, doing it for the whole crew. Doing the work so that someone else gains is <vocabulary form="やってあげる">to do (for someone)</vocabulary>, the outward giving inside <reading>やってあげる</reading>.

yatte-kureru.meaning_mnemonic: Back on the <reading>yacht, a crew</reading> of borrowed hands bails the flooded hull while you only hold the tiller. Someone else doing the work for you, while you sit back, is <vocabulary form="やってくれる">to do (for me)</vocabulary>, the inward favour inside <reading>やってくれる</reading>.

yatte-morau.meaning_mnemonic: Off the <reading>yacht, a moray</reading> eel is the only thing that will chew the fouled anchor rope free, so down it goes to do the job. Getting someone else to do the work in your place is <vocabulary form="やってもらう">to have (someone) do</vocabulary>, the sound sitting inside <reading>やってもらう</reading>.

yattsu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>eight</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>eight things</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
yattsu.reading_mnemonic: A toy <reading>yacht</reading> capsizes on the riverbank and spills <vocabulary>eight things</vocabulary> into the current. The kid wading after it yells <reading>やっつ</reading> as they float away.

yobu.meaning_mnemonic: Shout a name across the room and the person turns; say it warmly with a date attached and they show up to dinner. Both are one verb: to <vocabulary>call or invite</vocabulary> someone.
yobu.reading_mnemonic: Koichi leans out the konbini door and shouts <reading>yo, boo</reading> at every regular he spots on the street. To <reading>よぶ</reading> is to <vocabulary>call someone over</vocabulary> until they come in.

yoi.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the plain word for good pulling on a stiff, pressed suit. The い ending still makes it an adjective, but that starch is what turns it into <vocabulary>good (formal)</vocabulary>, the version for letters and speeches.
yoi.reading_mnemonic: A ship's lookout leans from the crow's nest and calls a long <reading>yo-eee</reading> each time the water ahead runs clear. That all-clear cry is 「<reading>よい</reading>」, the formal word for conditions that are <vocabulary>good (formal)</vocabulary>.

yokin.meaning_mnemonic: Hand your gold coins across the bank counter for safe keeping instead of spending them, and the <kanji form="金">money</kanji> the bank now holds for you is your <vocabulary form="預金">savings / deposit</vocabulary>.

yokka.meaning_mnemonic: Pacing off all <kanji>four</kanji> walls of that doorless room already burns a whole <kanji>day</kanji>. Four walls at a day apiece add up to <vocabulary>four days</vocabulary>.

yoku.meaning_mnemonic: The old ox at the riverbank has worn its <reading>yoke</reading> so <reading>よく</reading>, day after day, that it now ploughs a straight furrow <vocabulary>well</vocabulary> without a hand on the reins.

yomeru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="読">read</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="読める">can read</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they point at the same meaning. The extra ending just moves it from reading to being able to read.
yomeru.reading_mnemonic: You already know 読 is read 「よ」 from 読む, so <vocabulary form="読める">can read</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>よめる</reading>.

yomu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>read</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to read</vocabulary> word are one and the same, so the meaning carries straight over.
yomu.reading_mnemonic: A cow sits by the vending machine at the top of the mountain trail with the manual open. It works down the page going <reading>you moo</reading> at each line, because <reading>よむ</reading> is the cow's one skill, <vocabulary>to read</vocabulary>.

yon-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>four</kanji> kanji is the <vocabulary>four</vocabulary> word — nothing added, nothing changed to get here.
yon-v.reading_mnemonic: At the vending machine on the mountain trail, a hiker counts his water bottles. His huge <reading>yawn</reading> comes out sounding just like <reading>よん</reading> — he's short exactly <vocabulary>four</vocabulary>.
yon-v.description: Native speakers use this reading rather than the kanji's other reading, because that other reading sounds identical to the word for death and is avoided when counting aloud, especially in hospitals and elevators.

yorokobu.meaning_mnemonic: Hand someone the news they have been hoping for and watch them <kanji form="喜">rejoice</kanji>, all grin and thank-yous and a little bounce. That whole warm rush when something goes right for you is being <vocabulary form="喜ぶ">pleased</vocabulary>.
yorokobu.reading_mnemonic: Koichi slides <reading>your cocoa</reading> across the konbini counter on the cold morning you needed it most, and you light up before it lands. That instant lift when a good thing reaches your hands is 「<reading>よろこぶ</reading>」, <vocabulary form="喜ぶ">to be pleased</vocabulary>.

yoroshiku.meaning_mnemonic: On the two-person boat the deal is simple: <reading>you row, she cooks</reading>. You shake on it and say <reading>よろしく</reading>, asking her to <vocabulary form="よろしく">please treat me well</vocabulary>.

yoru.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's school gates lock shut the moment <vocabulary>night</vocabulary> falls, leaving the sports field dark and silent.
yoru.reading_mnemonic: A ghost at the riverbank moans 「<reading>よる</reading>」, which sounds just like calling <reading>your</reading> name, right as <vocabulary>night</vocabulary> falls.

yosan.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="算">calculate</kanji> <kanji form="予">beforehand</kanji> the exact yen a project is allowed to spend all year, and that fixed ceiling is its <vocabulary form="予算">budget</vocabulary>.

yotei.meaning_mnemonic: A time you <kanji>fix</kanji> in place <kanji>beforehand</kanji> so the day cannot drift is a <vocabulary>plan / schedule</vocabulary>.

yottsu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>four</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>four things</vocabulary> word share the same number, but the added つ turns a bare digit into four items you can point at and count.
yottsu.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a collector proudly shows off four half-sunk <reading>yachts</reading>, insisting that's exactly why everyone says <reading>よっつ</reading> when they mean <vocabulary>four things</vocabulary>.

youji.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>matter</kanji> you have to leave the house and settle face to face is an <vocabulary>errand</vocabulary>.

youka.meaning_mnemonic: Flip the calendar past <kanji>eight</kanji> pages, each one a <kanji>day</kanji>, and you have flipped through <vocabulary>eight days</vocabulary>.

youshoku.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="洋">ocean</kanji> here carries its other sense, foreign. So <kanji form="食">food</kanji> that came from across the water, the fried and buttery knife-and-fork kind, is <vocabulary form="洋食">Western food</vocabulary>.

yowai.meaning_mnemonic: You rest one elbow on the wire shelf by the konbini door and the whole rack folds to the floor, onigiri and all. A thing that gives out the moment anything leans on it is <vocabulary>weak</vocabulary>.
yowai.reading_mnemonic: A shrine kitten takes a run at the bottom mossy step, slides back down on its nose, and gives up. Grandma Kane watches and mutters <reading>'yo, why'</reading> bother, since a cat that <reading>よわい</reading> is exactly what <vocabulary>weak</vocabulary> looks like.

yoyaku-suru.meaning_mnemonic: You lock in a <kanji>promise</kanji>, made well <kanji>beforehand</kanji>, that one seat stays empty for you and nobody else. Getting that promise on the books is how you <vocabulary>reserve</vocabulary> it.

yubiwa.meaning_mnemonic: A metal band sized to slide onto one <kanji form="指">finger</kanji> and stay there is a <vocabulary form="指輪">ring</vocabulary> you wear as jewelry.

yuki.meaning_mnemonic: Rain that dawdled on the way down until it froze arrives as soft white clumps on your collar. That heaped, silent pile is <vocabulary>snow</vocabulary>.
yuki.reading_mnemonic: A kid trudges down the mountain trail with both boots packed full of half-melted <vocabulary>snow</vocabulary>. Every squelching step makes her groan 「<reading>ゆき</reading>」, and she is right, because that is genuinely <reading>yucky</reading>.

yukkuri.meaning_mnemonic: You wave Ree back from the beeping till with a calm <reading>ゆっくり</reading>. It is <reading>'you cook, Ree'</reading> at any pace, so the onigiri warms <vocabulary>slowly / leisurely</vocabulary>.

yume.meaning_mnemonic: The film that runs behind your eyes while you sleep, so real you talk back to it, then gone the instant the alarm goes, is a <vocabulary>dream</vocabulary>.
yume.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane bends over the sleeping cats on the shrine steps and whispers 「<reading>ゆめ</reading>」. <reading>You may</reading> fly, you may be rich, she means, but only until dawn, because none of it is real, it is just a <vocabulary>dream</vocabulary>.

yunyuu.meaning_mnemonic: When a cargo ship <kanji>send</kanji>s foreign goods across the sea and they <kanji>enter</kanji> your shops, what just landed is an <vocabulary>import</vocabulary>.

yurui.meaning_mnemonic: The elastic in Sei's gym shorts has lost all its stretch. One jog down the field and the waistband slides past his hips, flapping <vocabulary form="緩い">loose / lax</vocabulary> with every step.
yurui.reading_mnemonic: The knots Yuri ties never hold. Ask him to tie down a load and the rope stays <vocabulary form="緩い">loose / lax</vocabulary>, so the whole crew now calls a sloppy knot a <reading>ゆるい</reading> one, after <reading>Yuri</reading>.

yushutsu.meaning_mnemonic: Goods you <kanji>transport</kanji> to the country's <kanji>exit</kanji> and push out across the border are an <vocabulary>export</vocabulary>.

yuubinkyoku.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>facility</kanji> that handles <kanji>mail</kanji> and refuses to handle anything else is a <vocabulary>post office</vocabulary>.

yuugata.meaning_mnemonic: Every person on the street turns to face the same <kanji>direction</kanji> as the light fades, and that turning hour is <vocabulary>evening</vocabulary>.

yuujin.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>person</kanji> you would call a <kanji>friend</kanji>, named in the stiff wording you would put on a form, is a <vocabulary>friend (formal)</vocabulary>.

yuumei.meaning_mnemonic: Even with your face hidden, a <kanji>name</kanji> that this many strangers already <kanji>have</kanji> in their heads makes you <vocabulary>famous</vocabulary>. It takes な before the noun it describes.

zangyou.meaning_mnemonic: The office lights go off but part of the day's <kanji form="業">business</kanji> still <kanji form="残">remains</kanji> on your desk. The extra hour you stay to clear it is <vocabulary form="残業">overtime work</vocabulary>.

zannen.meaning_mnemonic: The one <kanji form="念">wish</kanji> you never acted on is the part that <kanji form="残">remains</kanji> unburied after the chance is gone. That is what <vocabulary form="残念">regrettable</vocabulary> names, and as a な adjective it takes な before its noun.

zasshi.meaning_mnemonic: Bind a fat stack of <kanji>miscellaneous</kanji> articles into a single glossy <kanji>document</kanji> and you have printed a <vocabulary>magazine</vocabulary>.

zehi.meaning_mnemonic: You hesitate on the step, and the innkeeper throws the door wide with a bright <reading>Zee, hi</reading> and waves you straight in. That whole-hearted come-right-in is <reading>ぜひ</reading>, <vocabulary form="ぜひ">by all means</vocabulary>.

zeikin.meaning_mnemonic: The slice of everyone's <kanji>money</kanji> that the government quietly rakes off every year to pay for roads, schools and soldiers is <vocabulary>tax</vocabulary>.

zenbu.meaning_mnemonic: Pull together every single <kanji>section</kanji> of a thing, skip none, and what is left in your hands is the <vocabulary>whole</vocabulary> of it.

zenzen.meaning_mnemonic: You hunt every shelf at Koichi's konbini for any <kanji>sort of thing</kanji> that could count as breakfast. There is nothing like it in the whole shop, <vocabulary>(not) at all</vocabulary>.

zero.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's team loses eleven to nothing, and the scoreboard just flashes the English word for it: <vocabulary>zero</vocabulary>.

zou.meaning_mnemonic: Behind the zoo fence stands a grey animal the size of a truck, its legs like pillars and its nose long enough to pick a bun off the ground. That reaching nose alone means <vocabulary form="象">elephant</vocabulary>.

zubon.meaning_mnemonic: Sit down, feed one leg in and then the other, and <reading>zip on</reading> the two cloth tubes. Fastened at your waist, that pair of tubes is <reading>ズボン</reading>, your <vocabulary form="ズボン">trousers</vocabulary>.

zurui.meaning_mnemonic: Every Sunday a kid runs the same <reading>zoo ruse</reading> and slips through a gap in the fence without paying. Beating the queue that way is <vocabulary form="ずるい">sly / unfair</vocabulary>, and the gate guard just sighs <reading>ずるい</reading>.
